subject: Science
title: Arun and Priya's Shadow Theater
hook: Can you make shadows dance? Arun and Priya explore light and dark.

slides.title: The Puppet Show
slides.storyContext: On a rainy evening, Arun and Priya set up a shadow puppet show. Priya holds a lamp. Arun makes hand shapes between the lamp and a white sheet. Giant shadows dance on the wall. 'How does this work?' asks Arun.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Arun's house. White sheet hung on wall. Lamp behind Arun. Dark room.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light makes shadows when blocked by objects.

image.alt: The Puppet Show — Light and Shadow

slides.title: What is Light?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'Light travels in straight lines from a source (like the sun or a lamp). When light hits an object, it can pass through (transparent), bend through (transparent-ish), or bounce off (opaque/reflective).'

points.label: Transparent
points.text: Light passes through—you see clearly (glass, water)

points.label: Translucent
points.text: Light bends through—blurry view (frosted glass)

points.label: Opaque
points.text: Light bounces off—you cannot see through (wood, paper)

slides.inSimpleWords: Light travels straight and bounces off things.

image.alt: What is Light? — Light and Shadow

slides.title: How Shadows Form
slides.storyContext: Arun holds his hand up to the lamp. 'Light goes straight from the lamp, hits my hand (opaque), and cannot go through. Behind my hand, there is no light—a shadow!'

example.problem: Why is there a shadow behind an opaque object in a light beam?
example.solution: Light travels in straight lines. When it hits an opaque object, it cannot pass through, creating a dark area (shadow) behind it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadows form when objects block light rays.

image.alt: How Shadows Form — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Shadow Sizes Change
slides.storyContext: Priya moves the lamp closer to Arun's hand. His shadow gets bigger. 'The closer the light source, the bigger the shadow because light spreads out from a point!'

points.label: Close light
points.text: Bigger shadow

points.label: Far light
points.text: Smaller shadow

points.label: Reason
points.text: Light rays spread wider from close source

slides.inSimpleWords: Light distance changes the size of shadows.

image.alt: Shadow Sizes Change — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Sun Shadows During the Day
slides.storyContext: Priya says, 'The sun creates your shadow outdoors. In the morning, your shadow is long. At noon, it is short. In the evening, it is long again. Why?' Arun figures out: 'Because the sun is angle changes!'

example.problem: Why is your shadow longest in early morning and late evening?
example.solution: When the sun is low on the horizon, light rays hit at an angle, making shadows stretch. At noon, the sun is high, shadows are short.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sun angle changes shadow size throughout the day.

image.alt: Sun Shadows During the Day — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Reflection: Light Bounces
slides.storyContext: Priya holds a mirror in Arun's light beam. 'Look! The light bounces off the mirror and reflects. Mirrors are very smooth and shiny, so light bounces perfectly.'

points.label: Reflection
points.text: Light bounces off smooth, shiny surfaces (mirrors)

points.label: Angle
points.text: Light bounces at the same angle it hits (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)

points.label: Diffuse
points.text: Rough surfaces scatter light in all directions

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors reflect light back instead of absorbing it.

image.alt: Reflection: Light Bounces — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Create Shadow Art
slides.storyContext: Arun and Priya stage a shadow puppet show: a dog, a butterfly, a bird. 'Make bigger shadows, smaller shadows, moving shadows!' says Priya. Arun practices different hand shapes and lamp distances.

points.label: Try this
points.text: Make 5 different animal shadows using your hands and a light source.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadow puppets show how light and objects interact.

image.alt: Create Shadow Art — Light and Shadow

slides.title: Light and Shadow Mastery
slides.storyContext: By night's end, Arun and Priya have created a complete puppet story. They now know: light travels straight, shadows form when light is blocked, and mirrors reflect light. Magic is just science!

points.label: Remember
points.text: Light travels in straight lines from a source

points.label: Remember
points.text: Shadows form behind opaque objects blocking light

points.label: Remember
points.text: Shadow size depends on light distance and angle

points.label: Remember
points.text: Mirrors reflect light; rough surfaces scatter it

slides.inSimpleWords: Light, shadows, and reflection create amazing effects.

image.alt: Light and Shadow Mastery — Light and Shadow

subject: English
title: Priya's Mystery Adventure
hook: Help Priya understand stories by asking the right questions

slides.title: Reading Comprehension
slides.storyContext: Priya sits with her grandmother in their village home. The monsoon rain taps on the roof. Daadiji opens an old book of folktales.
slides.inSimpleWords: Learning to understand and enjoy the stories you read.

image.alt: Reading Comprehension — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: The Mystery of the Lost Parrot
slides.storyContext: One morning, Priya reads a story in her textbook: 'Karan found a colorful parrot sitting on his window. He gave it water and seeds. The next day, the parrot flew away and brought a friend. Now Karan had two parrots.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A story is like a gift—read it slowly, watch what happens, and think about why.

image.alt: The Mystery of the Lost Parrot — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Reading is a Skill
slides.storyContext: Daadiji explains to Priya: 'Reading is not just pronouncing words. It's understanding what the author is saying, seeing pictures in your mind, and feeling the story.'

points.text: Reading = recognizing words + understanding meaning + enjoying the story

slides.inSimpleWords: Good reading means truly understanding the story!

slides.title: Who, What, Where, When
slides.storyContext: Daadiji asks Priya questions about the parrot story. Priya learns to spot the main details.

points.label: Who
points.text: The people or animals in the story (Karan and the parrots)

points.label: What
points.text: What happens in the story (a parrot visits, then brings a friend)

points.label: Where
points.text: Where the story takes place (on Karan's window)

points.label: When
points.text: The time of the story (morning, then next day)

slides.inSimpleWords: Always ask these 4 questions to understand any story.

image.alt: Who, What, Where, When — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Who and What Practice
slides.storyContext: Priya reads a new story: 'Meera and her dog Tippy went to the park. They played fetch all afternoon. Tippy caught the ball every time!'

example.problem: Who is the story about and what do they do?
example.solution: WHO: Meera and her dog Tippy. WHAT: They go to the park and play fetch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always find who and what first!

slides.title: The Main Idea
slides.storyContext: Sunny barks at a lizard on the wall. Priya thinks: 'This is a small detail. The BIG idea in the parrot story is: kindness brings friendship.'

points.text: A story has a main idea—the most important thing that happens
Small details support the main idea (Karan gave water and seeds)
The main idea teaches us something (be kind to animals)

slides.inSimpleWords: The main idea is like the heart of the story; everything else supports it.

image.alt: The Main Idea — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Finding the Main Idea
slides.storyContext: Daadiji asks Priya: 'In the Meera story, what is the main idea?' Priya thinks: 'Meera loves her dog very much. They have fun together.' Daadiji nods. 'That's the heart!'

example.problem: What is the main idea of the Meera story?
example.solution: The main idea is that Meera and Tippy share a strong bond and love playing together. The specific detail (playing fetch) supports this big idea.

slides.inSimpleWords: Main idea equals the most important message!

slides.title: Finding the Order of Events
slides.storyContext: Priya uses three stones to mark: First stone (Karan finds parrot), middle stone (he gives food), last stone (parrot brings a friend). This is the order things happen.

points.text: Events happen in order: first, then, finally
Words like 'morning', 'next day', 'then' show order
Knowing the order helps you understand the story better

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories move forward like steps up a ladder—one thing after another.

image.alt: Finding the Order of Events — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Story Sequencing
slides.storyContext: Priya learns to spot order words: 'Once', 'Then', 'Next', 'Finally', 'Meanwhile', 'At last'. These words tell her when things happen. Without order, stories become confusing!

points.text: Order words are clues. They show the story's timeline.

slides.inSimpleWords: Order words guide us through the story!

slides.title: Understanding Feelings
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'How did Karan feel when the parrot came back with a friend?' Daadiji smiles: 'His heart was full of joy! He loved the animals even more.'

points.text: Characters have feelings (happy, sad, scared, excited)
We know their feelings from what they DO (Karan gave food equals he cares)
Understanding feelings helps us like the story more

slides.inSimpleWords: Good readers feel what the characters feel.

image.alt: Understanding Feelings — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Feelings from Actions
slides.storyContext: Daadiji reads: 'Asha saw her mother crying. She ran and hugged her tight. She brought her a glass of water and sat beside her.' Priya says, 'Asha must love her very much!'

example.problem: How do we know Asha's feelings if the author doesn't say them?
example.solution: From her actions! She hugs her mother, brings water, and sits beside her. These actions show love and care.

slides.inSimpleWords: Actions reveal character feelings!

slides.title: Cause and Effect
slides.storyContext: Priya learns: 'WHY did the parrot fly away? BECAUSE Karan was kind. That's cause and effect—why something happens.'

points.text: Cause equals WHY something happens
Effect equals WHAT happens as a result
Understanding cause-effect makes stories make sense

slides.inSimpleWords: Cause is why; effect is what happens!

slides.title: Read and Answer
slides.storyContext: Daadiji gives Priya a short story to practice: 'Meera went to the market with her mother. She saw a stall with colorful ribbons. She chose a blue ribbon for her sister's hair. Her sister danced with joy.'

example.problem: Read the story and tell: (1) Who is the main person? (2) What did Meera do? (3) Where did it happen? (4) How did Meera's sister feel?
example.solution: (1) Meera. (2) She went to the market and bought a blue ribbon. (3) At the market. (4) Happy and joyful—she danced!

slides.inSimpleWords: Always ask WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN to answer questions about stories.

image.alt: Read and Answer — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Details vs Main Idea
slides.storyContext: Priya struggles. She writes down every tiny detail: 'Karan wore red shirt. The window had blue paint. The parrot was green.' Daadiji says, 'Those are nice details, but what's the MAIN point?' Priya realizes: 'Kindness brings friends!'

points.text: Details equal small facts. Main idea equals big message.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep the main idea central; details support it!

slides.title: Your Turn: Mini Story
slides.storyContext: Priya's teacher gives her a short passage: 'Ram liked to play cricket. One day, he broke the ball. He felt sad. But his friend Asha gave him a new ball. Ram was very happy. They played together until sunset.'

example.problem: Answer: (1) What was the problem? (2) How was it solved? (3) What is the main idea?
example.solution: (1) Ram broke his ball. (2) Asha gave him a new ball. (3) Real friends help when we are sad.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read carefully, ask questions, and think about what the story teaches.

image.alt: Your Turn: Mini Story — Reading Comprehension

slides.title: Practice Passage: The Lost Bicycle
slides.storyContext: Priya reads: 'Rahul lost his bicycle keys. He looked everywhere for an hour. He felt worried. Then his neighbor Mr. Khan found the keys under a bush. He returned them to Rahul. Rahul thanked him with a smile.'

example.problem: Answer: (1) Who? (2) What problem? (3) Where? (4) Main idea?
example.solution: (1) Rahul and Mr. Khan. (2) Lost bicycle keys. (3) Rahul's neighborhood. (4) Kindness of neighbors helps in time of need.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice asking all the questions!

slides.title: Inferencing: Reading Between Lines
slides.storyContext: Daadiji says: 'Sometimes authors don't say everything. We must INFER—guess what they mean based on clues.' Priya reads: 'Ravi's eyes were wet. His voice was shaky.' Priya infers, 'He must be sad or scared.'

points.text: Inference equals using clues to guess what isn't said
Good readers use text clues plus their own experience

slides.inSimpleWords: Read between the lines to understand deeper meaning!

slides.title: Inference Practice
slides.storyContext: Priya reads: 'Manju hadn't eaten all day. Her mother made her favorite khichdi. Manju's nose twitched. A smile spread across her face.' Priya infers: 'Manju was hungry and happy to see her favorite food!'

example.problem: What can we infer about Manju from the clues?
example.solution: She was hungry (hadn't eaten all day). She was happy and excited (nose twitched, smiled). She loves khichdi (mother made her favorite).

slides.inSimpleWords: Clues help us infer character feelings and situations!

slides.title: Vocabulary from Context
slides.storyContext: Priya encounters a new word: 'The old castle stood majestically on the hill, its grand towers reaching toward the sky.' She guesses, 'Majestically means impressively or beautifully, because castles are impressive places.'

points.text: When you see a new word, look at other words around it for clues
Context helps you guess the meaning without a dictionary

slides.inSimpleWords: Context clues help you understand new words!

slides.title: Preview Before Reading
slides.storyContext: Daadiji teaches Priya: 'Before you read, preview! Look at the title, pictures, and first sentence. This gives you clues about what the story will be.'

points.text: Previewing helps prepare your mind for the story.

slides.inSimpleWords: Preview like peeking at a gift before opening!

slides.title: Summarizing a Story
slides.storyContext: After reading, Priya summarizes: 'The story is about Karan who was kind to a parrot, and it brought him friendship.' That's a summary—the main points in your own words.

points.text: Summary = main idea + key events in fewer words

slides.inSimpleWords: A summary is the story in a nutshell!

slides.title: Story Summary Practice
slides.storyContext: Daadiji reads a story about a girl who plants a seed, watches it grow, and shares the flowers. Priya summarizes: 'A girl's kindness (planting a gift) brings joy to her community (sharing flowers).'

example.problem: Summarize this story in 1-2 sentences.
example.solution: A girl plants a seed with love and care. The flowers that grow bring happiness to everyone around her.

slides.inSimpleWords: Summaries capture the heart of the story!

slides.title: Compare and Contrast Stories
slides.storyContext: Priya reads two stories: one about Karan with a parrot, one about Meera with her dog. Daadiji asks, 'How are they alike? Different?' Priya sees both are about kindness, but different animals.

points.text: Comparing = finding similarities. Contrasting = finding differences.

slides.inSimpleWords: See how stories are same and different!

slides.title: Fiction vs Non-Fiction
slides.storyContext: Daadiji shows Priya two books. 'This one has imaginary animals talking—that's fiction. This one teaches real facts about animals—that's non-fiction. Different types, different purposes!'

points.text: Fiction = made-up stories. Non-fiction = real facts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fiction is imaginary; non-fiction is real!

slides.title: Write Your Own Story
slides.storyContext: Daadiji challenges Priya: 'Now YOU write a story! Remember: have characters, setting, events, and a main idea. Make it interesting!' Priya writes about Sunny helping a lost child find home.

example.problem: Can you create your own story with characters and a main idea?
example.solution: Yes! Your story should have: WHO (characters), WHERE (setting), WHAT (plot), and a main idea (message or lesson).

slides.inSimpleWords: You can be an author too!

slides.title: How to Understand Stories

points.text: Ask WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN to find key details
Find the main idea—what the story is really about
Notice the order of events (first, then, finally)
Understand how characters feel through their actions
Look for cause and effect (why things happen)
Infer meaning from clues when author doesn't say it
Use context to understand new words
Preview before reading and summarize after
Good readers ask questions and think deeply

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading is like detective work—look for clues and understand the whole picture!

subject: English
title: Anaya's Special Letters
hook: Write kind letters to friends and family the right way

characters.name: Grandpa
characters.role: lives far away in another city

slides.title: Letter Writing
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother shows her a blue envelope. Inside is a handwritten letter from Grandpa in Delhi, asking about her school life. Anaya wants to write back.
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are friendly messages we write by hand to someone we care about.

image.alt: Letter Writing — Letter Writing

slides.title: Why We Write Letters
slides.storyContext: Anaya learned that Grandpa's eyes get tired on his computer. A paper letter makes him very happy because he can hold it, read it slowly, and keep it forever. Her mother says: 'Your words on paper are like a warm hug.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters show people we care, and they treasure them.

image.alt: Why We Write Letters — Letter Writing

slides.title: Letters Are Special Gifts
slides.storyContext: Anaya sits with her mother and listens: 'Letters are different from emails or messages. They take time. They feel real. People keep them in boxes and read them again and again, remembering your love. When you write a letter, you give someone the best gift—your thought and your heart.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A letter is a present that keeps giving, every time the reader opens it.

slides.title: Parts of a Friendly Letter
slides.storyContext: Anaya sits at the kitchen table with pencil and paper. Her mother shows her the five parts of a letter using her fingers.

points.label: Date
points.text: Write the day at the top (e.g., 15 June 2026)

points.label: Greeting
points.text: Start with 'Dear Grandpa,' or 'Hello Ria,'

points.label: Body
points.text: Tell your news and feelings (2-3 sentences)

points.label: Closing
points.text: End with 'Your loving granddaughter,' or 'With love,'

points.label: Signature
points.text: Sign your name below the closing

slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter has five parts—like a body has head, arms, and legs.

image.alt: Parts of a Friendly Letter — Letter Writing

slides.title: Anaya's First Try
slides.storyContext: Anaya picks up her pencil. 'I'm nervous,' she whispers. Her mother smiles: 'You know what to do. You have five boxes to fill. Box 1: the date. Box 2: say hello. Box 3: tell your story. Box 4: say goodbye. Box 5: sign your name. Go!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter is a simple puzzle—five boxes, and your heart fills them.

slides.title: Writing the Date and Greeting
slides.storyContext: Anaya writes on her paper: '20 June 2026' at the top. Then she skips a line and writes: 'Dear Grandpa,'

points.text: Write today's date on the first line
Use a comma after the person's name in the greeting
Keep it warm but respectful (Dear, Hello, Hi work fine)

slides.inSimpleWords: The date and greeting welcome the reader into your letter.

image.alt: Writing the Date and Greeting — Letter Writing

slides.title: Date and Greeting in Action
slides.storyContext: Anaya's pencil moves: '20 June 2026' on the first line, blank line, then 'Dear Grandpa,' She says it aloud: 'It sounds nice!'

example.problem: Write the date and greeting for a letter to your mother.
example.solution:
28 June 2026

Dear Mama,

slides.inSimpleWords: The date tells when you wrote it. The greeting is your 'hello.'

slides.title: The Body: Your Message
slides.storyContext: Anaya writes: 'I hope you are well. I got 95 in my maths test today! I also played a new game at school called Tag. My friend Ria and I won our team. I miss you very much.'

points.text: Share real news from your life (school, friends, hobbies)
Use simple, clear sentences (2-4 sentences is perfect)
Tell how you feel (happy, proud, sad, excited)
Ask about the other person (How are you? What are you doing?)

slides.inSimpleWords: The body is your heart—share what matters to you.

image.alt: The Body: Your Message — Letter Writing

slides.title: What Should I Say?
slides.storyContext: Anaya bites her pencil. 'What do I write about, Mama?' Her mother laughs: 'Think of what made you happy today. Did you learn something? Did you play with a friend? Did you try something new? Tell Grandpa these things. Tell him three good things. Then ask him one question. That's enough!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your body tells a story—your day, your feelings, your questions.

slides.title: Body Examples for Different People
slides.storyContext: Anaya looks at what other kids wrote in their bodies:

example.problem: What are two good body paragraphs?
example.solution:
To Grandpa: 'I won the spelling bee! My team beat Class 4. I wish you were here to see it. How is your garden growing?'

To friend Ria: 'We made art today with paints and paper. I made a butterfly. It was so fun! Can you come play after school tomorrow?'

slides.inSimpleWords: Different people, different messages—but always true and warm.

slides.title: The Closing and Signature
slides.storyContext: Anaya finishes writing: 'With lots of love, Anaya' at the bottom. She reads it aloud, and it sounds just right.

points.text: Choose a warm closing: 'With love,', 'Your loving...', 'All my love,'
Skip a line and write your name
Your signature shows the letter came from your heart

slides.inSimpleWords: The closing is a hug—it shows you care.

image.alt: The Closing and Signature — Letter Writing

slides.title: Signing with Your Whole Heart
slides.storyContext: Anaya holds her pencil high. 'My name is Anaya,' she says proudly, writing each letter slowly. Her mother says: 'When you sign, you're saying to Grandpa: this letter is really from me, really from my heart, really from my hands. Your name is your promise.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your signature is your stamp—it means 'This is really from me.'

slides.title: Closings That Work Best

points.label: For Grandparents
points.text: 'With lots of love,' or 'Your loving granddaughter,'

points.label: For Friends
points.text: 'Your best friend,' or 'With giggles,'

points.label: For Teachers
points.text: 'Respectfully,' or 'Your student,'

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose a closing that fits the person and how you feel.

slides.title: A Real Letter from Anaya
slides.storyContext: Here is the complete letter Anaya wrote to Grandpa.

example.problem: Write a friendly letter following all five parts.
example.solution:
20 June 2026

Dear Grandpa,

I hope you are well. I got 95 in my maths test today! I played cricket at school and scored 20 runs. I miss you so much and want you to visit soon. How are you? Are you eating well?

With lots of love,
Anaya

slides.inSimpleWords: A good letter is honest, warm, and easy to read.

image.alt: A Real Letter from Anaya — Letter Writing

slides.title: The Envelope and the Stamp
slides.storyContext: Anaya folds her letter carefully. Her mother shows her how to address an envelope: 'Top left is your name. Bottom right is Grandpa's name and city. The stamp goes top right. It's like the letter's travel ticket!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The envelope carries your words safely to someone far away.

slides.title: Write Your Own Letter
slides.storyContext: Ria's birthday is coming. Anaya decides to write her a birthday letter. 'I want to tell her how special she is to me,' Anaya thinks.

example.problem: Write a short friendly letter to a friend, including all five parts. Share a happy memory or tell them why they are special.
example.solution:
15 July 2026

Dear Ria,

Happy birthday to my best friend! I remember when we first met in Class 1 and we shared our lunch. Now we play together every day. You make me laugh and you are kind to everyone. I am so lucky to have you as a friend. Let's have fun at your birthday party!

With love,
Anaya

slides.inSimpleWords: When you write a letter, imagine sitting with the person and talking to them.

image.alt: Write Your Own Letter — Letter Writing

slides.title: Grandpa Writes Back
slides.storyContext: One week later, Anaya comes home to find a blue envelope on the table. Her mother gives it to her with a smile. Inside, Grandpa has written: 'Dear Anaya, Your letter made me the happiest grandpa in Delhi. I read it three times. I am proud of your maths. Come visit soon. Love, Grandpa'
slides.inSimpleWords: The best part of writing letters is the reply that comes back—proof that someone cares.

slides.title: Why Letters Matter More Than Messages

points.label: Take Time
points.text: They show you took the trouble to write by hand

points.label: Last Forever
points.text: People keep them in boxes and reread them years later

points.label: Feel Real
points.text: You can see your handwriting, smell the paper, hold it close

points.label: Show Love
points.text: Every word says 'You are worth my time and thought'

slides.inSimpleWords: Messages fade. Letters stay. Letters say 'I love you' louder than any text.

slides.title: Fix This Letter (Find the Mistakes)
slides.storyContext: Anaya's cousin Rohan wrote a letter but made mistakes. Can you spot them?

example.problem:
Find the five errors in this letter:

20 june 2026
Dear Ria
I had fun with you yesterday. We played. It was nice.
With love
Rohan
example.solution:
1. Month should be capitalized: June (not june)
2. Greeting needs a comma: Dear Ria, (not Dear Ria)
3. Body is too short—add details!
4. Closing needs a comma: With love, (not With love)
5. Add a line break before signature

slides.inSimpleWords: Good letters have details, proper punctuation, and warmth.

slides.title: Letters Across India
slides.storyContext: Anaya learns that her grandmother in Mumbai, her aunt in Bangalore, and her cousin in Hyderabad all treasure the letters they get. 'Letters connect us,' her mother says. 'When someone lives far away, a letter is like a bridge of words bringing them close again.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters travel across deserts and mountains to touch someone's heart.

slides.title: Anaya Becomes a Letter Writer
slides.storyContext: By the end of summer, Anaya has written letters to Grandpa, Ria, her teacher, and her aunt. People smile when they see her name on an envelope. 'You have a gift,' her mother says, 'for making people feel loved.' Anaya beams with pride.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you write letters, you become a giver of happiness.

slides.title: Challenge: Write to Someone New
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. Think of someone you love or admire—maybe a cousin, uncle, teacher, or friend. Write them a letter using all five parts. Make it warm and honest.

example.problem: Choose a person and write a complete five-part letter to them.
example.solution: Remember: Date, Greeting, Body (3-4 sentences with real news), Closing, and Signature. Take your time. Your words matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter you write is an act of love—don't be shy.

slides.title: Letters Through History
slides.storyContext: Anaya's grandmother shows her a stack of old letters tied with ribbon. These are from her mother, Anaya's great-grandmother. She lived in a village without phones or internet. These letters kept us connected across hundreds of miles. Anaya holds them carefully, feeling the weight of love across generations.
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are time capsules of love—they last forever.

slides.title: Special Types of Letters

points.label: Thank-You Letters
points.text: Express gratitude for a gift, help, or kind gesture

points.label: Apology Letters
points.text: Say sorry, explain why, and promise to do better

points.label: Love Letters
points.text: Tell someone how much they mean to you

points.label: Birthday Letters
points.text: Celebrate someone's special day in a personal way

slides.inSimpleWords: Each type of letter has its own warmth and purpose.

slides.title: Mix and Match Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya gets creative. She decides to write three different types of letters in one day.

example.problem: Write: (1) a thank-you letter to a teacher, (2) an apology letter to a friend, (3) a birthday letter to a sibling.
example.solution: Each should follow the five parts but with different tones. Thank-you: warm and grateful. Apology: honest and sincere. Birthday: joyful and celebratory.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice different letter types—become a master letter writer.

slides.title: Anaya's Letter Legacy
slides.storyContext: Years later, Anaya's friends and family will treasure her letters. Her grandpa will reread her letters during lonely nights. Her best friend will keep them in a box. Her mother will show them to Anaya's children someday and say: This is how your mother loved us.
slides.inSimpleWords: Your letters today become someone's treasure tomorrow.

slides.title: Five Steps to Write a Letter

points.text: Write the date at the top
Use a greeting like 'Dear...' with a comma
Share real news and feelings in the body (2-4 sentences)
Close with a warm ending like 'With love,'
Sign your name—show it came from your heart

slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are love in an envelope—take time, be honest, and share your heart.
