subject: English
title: Vikram's Tale of the Clever Fox
hook: Enjoy stories full of adventure, animals, and life lessons

characters.name: Teacher Meera
characters.role: brings stories to life in class

slides.title: Story Reading
slides.storyContext: Vikram sits in the village library after school. Teacher Meera comes to him with a brown book of stories. 'Today, I have a story of a very clever fox,' she says, opening to the first page.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are journeys—take them with all your heart and imagination.

image.alt: Story Reading — Story Reading

slides.title: The Story Begins
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads: 'Once, a hungry fox came to a village. He saw a farmer's henhouse. But the gate had a lock. How would he get inside?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every story starts with 'once upon a time' and a problem to solve.

image.alt: The Story Begins — Story Reading

slides.title: The Fox's Journey (Middle of the Tale)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera continues: 'The fox tried to dig under the fence. He worked all night. By dawn, he had a tunnel. He squeezed through, closer and closer to the hens. But then—the farmer's dog barked! The fox's heart raced.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories rise and fall—they have exciting middles where things get tricky.

slides.title: Story Elements: Characters
slides.storyContext: Vikram learns that stories have heroes, villains, and helpers. The fox is clever and hungry. The farmer is kind but needs to protect his hens. The hens are innocent and scared.

points.text: Characters are the people and animals in the story
Main character (hero): the fox trying to solve a problem
Supporting characters: the farmer, the hens
Each character has feelings and reasons for what they do

slides.inSimpleWords: Characters are like people in real life—each one is different and special.

image.alt: Story Elements: Characters — Story Reading

slides.title: Know Your Characters
slides.storyContext: Vikram asks: 'But why does the fox want the hens?' Teacher Meera explains: 'He's hungry. Foxes hunt to survive. The farmer protects his hens because that's his job. Nobody is purely evil—they just have different needs.'

example.problem: Why does each character act the way they do?
example.solution:
Fox: He's hungry and wants to eat.
Farmer: He works hard and owns the hens—he must protect them.
Hens: They are scared because foxes hunt them.
Each character has a reason.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good stories show why people act the way they do.

slides.title: Story Elements: Plot (What Happens)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera shows Vikram the story's arc: Problem (fox hungry, henhouse locked) → Attempt (fox digs under the fence) → Climax (he almost gets in!) → Twist (farmer catches him!) → Ending (fox runs away and learns a lesson).

points.text: Problem: What is the challenge or trouble?
Rising Action: What does the character try? Does it work?
Climax: The most exciting or important moment
Ending: How is the problem solved? What lesson was learned?

slides.inSimpleWords: A plot is like climbing a hill—up, up, peak, then down to peace.

image.alt: Story Elements: Plot (What Happens) — Story Reading

slides.title: The Climax (Most Exciting Part)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera's voice gets loud and fast: 'The fox pushed through the tunnel. The hens screamed. The farmer ran out with a stick. The dog barked and barked. The fox turned and RAN! The farmer chased him all the way to the forest edge!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The climax is where everything shakes—where you hold your breath.

slides.title: Story Elements: Setting (Where and When)
slides.storyContext: The fox's story happens in a village at dawn. It takes place on the outskirts of a farm, near a henhouse, under a big mango tree. The time of year is summer when foxes are hungriest.

points.text: Setting tells WHERE the story happens (village, forest, house, city)
Setting tells WHEN it happens (morning, summer, long ago, today)
The setting affects what happens (a sleepy village is different from a busy market)

slides.inSimpleWords: Setting is the stage where the story dances—it shapes everything.

image.alt: Story Elements: Setting (Where and When) — Story Reading

slides.title: The Ending (What We Learn)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera's voice becomes calm and thoughtful: 'The fox sat in the forest, panting. He had tried so hard but failed. That night, he found a dead rabbit left by a hunter. He ate it and thought: sometimes trying to steal is harder and more dangerous than finding honest food. The fox learned that day.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Endings teach us—they show what happens when someone learns.

slides.title: The Lesson (Moral) of the Story
slides.storyContext: Vikram finishes reading and asks: 'What does this story teach us?' Teacher Meera smiles: 'The fox was clever, but being cunning doesn't always win. The farmer's honesty and kindness are stronger. Also, respecting others' things keeps you safe.'

points.text: Every good story has a lesson or moral (a teaching about life)
The lesson might be about kindness, honesty, hard work, or courage
The ending shows the lesson by what happens to the characters

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story whispers: 'This is how to live a good life.'

image.alt: The Lesson (Moral) of the Story — Story Reading

slides.title: A Complete Story for You
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads Vikram a short tale: 'There was a kind boy named Arjun. He found a hungry kitten on the street. He gave it milk and rice every day. Soon, the kitten became strong and healthy. It played with Arjun and they became best friends. The whole village loved them both.'

example.problem: Find: (1) Main character? (2) Setting? (3) Problem? (4) How was it solved? (5) What is the lesson?
example.solution: (1) Arjun and the kitten. (2) The street and Arjun's home. (3) Hungry kitten, lonely Arjun. (4) Arjun fed the kitten and cared for it. (5) Kindness brings friendship and happiness.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good stories show how kind hearts change the world.

image.alt: A Complete Story for You — Story Reading

slides.title: Stories Connect Us
slides.storyContext: After the story, Vikram asks Teacher Meera: 'Are there really clever foxes like that?' She smiles: 'Foxes do exist, and they are clever. But this story is also made up—it's a fable, a tale with a lesson. Thousands of children in India have read this same story. We all feel the same feelings when we read it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are bridges—they connect our hearts across time and place.

slides.title: Story Spot (Find the Elements)
slides.storyContext: Vikram reads a new short story: 'Priya lived in a small town by the river. One day, a storm came. The river flooded. Priya's neighbors were scared. She led everyone to the high ground of the old temple. All were safe. Priya became the village hero.'

example.problem: Identify: (1) Who is the hero? (2) What is the problem? (3) Where does it happen? (4) When does it happen? (5) What is the lesson?
example.solution: (1) Priya. (2) A flood from a storm. (3) A river town, at the temple. (4) During a storm/sudden crisis. (5) Courage and quick thinking save lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Great readers spot every part of a story—characters, plot, setting, and lesson.

image.alt: Story Spot (Find the Elements) — Story Reading

slides.title: Different Types of Stories

points.label: Fables
points.text: Short stories with animals that teach a moral (like the fox story)

points.label: Folktales
points.text: Old stories passed down through families and cultures

points.label: Adventures
points.text: Exciting stories with travel, danger, and heroism

points.label: Fairytales
points.text: Magical stories with princes, princesses, and magic

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories come in many flavors—each kind teaches or delights us differently.

slides.title: Vikram Becomes a Story Reader
slides.storyContext: Week after week, Vikram and Teacher Meera read together. He finds himself sitting under the mango tree with a book, lost in stories. He reads about princesses in palaces, animals in forests, and children solving mysteries. Each story teaches him something new about courage, kindness, and the world.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you start reading stories, you become a traveler to a thousand worlds.

slides.title: Retell a Story
slides.storyContext: Think of a story you know—from your family, your culture, or a book. Retell it to a friend using the story elements: Who are the characters? What is the problem? Where and when does it happen? What is the lesson?

example.problem: Retell a story using all four elements.
example.solution: Characters: (names/roles), Setting: (where and when), Problem: (the main trouble), Lesson: (what we learn)

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story you know is a gift—share it with others.

slides.title: Reading Creates Empathy
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera asks Vikram: 'When you read about the fox, you felt his hunger, his cunning, his disappointment. When you read about Priya, you felt her courage. This is empathy—you feel what the character feels. That makes you kinder in real life.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories teach us to feel what others feel.

slides.title: How to Read Deeper

points.label: Ask Why
points.text: Why does the character act this way? What do they want?

points.label: Notice Details
points.text: What does the story tell us about the setting, time, or mood?

points.label: Predict Ahead
points.text: What do you think will happen next? Why?

points.label: Reflect After
points.text: What did you learn? How does it change you?

slides.inSimpleWords: Deep reading means asking questions and thinking hard.

slides.title: Reading Practice: A Mystery Story
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads: 'A girl found a locked box in her attic. Inside was a letter from her great-grandmother. It said: I hid the truth about our family. Now you're old enough to know. The girl's hands shook.'

example.problem: Stop here and predict: What is the truth? What will the girl do next? What lesson might this story teach?
example.solution: Many answers are possible: She might discover a hidden relative, a secret talent, a forgotten recipe. The lesson might be about family, truth, or courage. That's what makes stories beautiful—we all imagine differently.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every reader imagines the story uniquely—that's the magic.

slides.title: Create Your Own Character
slides.storyContext: Now Vikram tries to create his own story character. He thinks: Who will my hero be? What do they want? What problem will they face?

example.problem: Invent a character. Write: (1) Their name and age, (2) What they want more than anything, (3) One strength, (4) One weakness, (5) A problem they face.
example.solution: Example: Asha, age 9, wants to be a cricket player. Strength: fast runner. Weakness: afraid to fail. Problem: her family says girls shouldn't play sports.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every good story starts with a person we care about.

slides.title: Stories Show Different Worlds
slides.storyContext: Vikram reads stories from different countries—folktales from Japan, Africa, South America. He learns that stories are universal. Every culture tells tales of courage, love, and wisdom.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories connect us to people everywhere.

slides.title: Story Mapping
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera teaches Vikram to map a story visually—drawing the beginning, middle, and end.

example.problem: Draw or write a story map: Left side (beginning: setting and characters), Middle (rising action and climax), Right side (resolution and lesson).
example.solution: The fox story: Beginning (fox hungry, henhouse locked), Middle (fox digs tunnel, almost gets in), Climax (farmer catches him), End (fox runs away, learns a lesson).

slides.inSimpleWords: Visual maps help you see the story's shape.

slides.title: Vikram's Reading Journey
slides.storyContext: By the end of summer, Vikram has read 20 stories. He can spot characters, plot twists, and lessons instantly. But more importantly, he loves stories. He reads before bed, at lunch, in the park. Stories are now part of his life.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you love reading, stories become your best friends.

slides.title: Write Your Own Short Story
slides.storyContext: Vikram is ready to write his own story. He has characters in mind, a problem, and an idea for an ending.

example.problem: Write a short story (5-10 sentences) with: a hero, a clear problem, at least one attempt to solve it, a climax, and a lesson.
example.solution: Story: A boy named Dev found a hurt bird. He made a nest, fed it, stayed with it all week. When it flew away, Dev felt sad but proud. He learned: sometimes love means letting go.

slides.inSimpleWords: You have all the tools—now tell your story.

slides.title: Stories Connect Hearts
slides.storyContext: Vikram realizes that when he reads a story, he's not alone. Thousands of children have read the same fox tale. They all laughed at the same moments, felt scared during the same climax, and learned the same lesson. Stories are like bridges connecting hearts across time.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you read a story, you join millions of readers across the world.

slides.title: Story Detective Challenge
slides.storyContext: Vikram becomes a Story Detective. He reads a new story and must solve five mysteries before moving on.

example.problem:
For any story you read, answer:
1. Who is the main character?
2. What do they want or need?
3. What stops them from getting it?
4. How do they overcome it?
5. What do they learn?
example.solution: These five questions unlock the heart of every story. Master them, and you can understand any tale.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story has secrets. Learn to find them.

slides.title: Real Stories vs. Made-Up Stories

points.label: Real Stories (Nonfiction)
points.text: True events that really happened—biographies, history, news

points.label: Made-Up Stories (Fiction)
points.text: Invented tales with imaginary characters and events

points.label: Mix
points.text: Some stories blend both—real events with added details or emotions

slides.inSimpleWords: Both real and imaginary stories teach us—in different ways.

slides.title: Vikram's Story Collection
slides.storyContext: By year's end, Vikram has read 30 stories. He keeps them all in his mind like a library. He can revisit them anytime. He tells them to his little sister at bedtime. He shares them with friends. Stories have become his superpower.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories you read stay with you forever—they shape who you become.

slides.title: How to Enjoy Stories

points.text: Learn the characters—understand their feelings and choices
Follow the plot—beginning, middle, end, and how it's solved
Notice the setting—where and when the story happens
Find the lesson—what the story teaches about life
Use imagination—picture the story like a movie in your mind

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are mirrors of life—read them slowly and let them speak to your heart.

image.alt: How to Enjoy Stories — Story Reading

subject: English
title: Maya's Rainbow of Words
hook: Feel the magic of poems that sing and dance

slides.title: Poetry
slides.storyContext: Rain falls on the roof of Maya's school. Poet Uncle visits Class 3 and opens a slim book of poems. 'Today, we feel with words!' he says, and reads: 'Pitter-patter, pitter-pat, raindrops dance on the mat.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is language playing music—words that sing, rhyme, and paint pictures.

image.alt: Poetry — Poetry

slides.title: Why Poets Write
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle tells Maya: 'I write poems to catch feelings in words. When I see a butterfly, I feel free. When I hear a child laugh, I feel joy. Poems say big feelings in small, beautiful ways. A poem is a gift of the heart.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poems let us say how we feel when words aren't enough.

image.alt: Why Poets Write — Poetry

slides.title: Poetry Lives Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle claps his hands: 'Poetry isn't just in books. It's in songs you hear on the radio. It's in nursery rhymes. It's in prayers. It's in a mother's lullaby. Listen! You'll find poetry hiding all around you.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry isn't rare—it's everywhere, singing if you listen closely.

slides.title: Rhyme: Words That Sound Alike
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle claps and reads: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, How I wonder what you are!' Maya claps too—'star' and 'are' sound the same!'

points.text: Rhyme is when two words sound alike at the end (cat, bat; moon, soon)
Rhyming words make poems fun to read and easy to remember
Rhyming patterns can be AABB (first two lines rhyme, next two rhyme) or ABAB

example.problem: Find the rhyming words: 'The cat sat on a mat, She wore a funny hat.'
example.solution: sat/mat rhyme (A), hat rhymes with them too. This is AAA rhyme.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyme is poetry's music—when words dance to the same beat.

image.alt: Rhyme: Words That Sound Alike — Poetry

slides.title: Rhyme Makes Us Remember
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle laughs: 'Do you know your ABCs? A-B-C-D-E-F-G... You remember it because it rhymes! When a poem rhymes, it sticks in your brain like glue. You can recite it months later!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyming poems are sticky—your brain loves them and remembers.

slides.title: Rhythm: The Heartbeat of Words
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle drums on the table: 'Boom-boom-BOOM, boom-boom-BOOM. Listen to the pattern.' Maya walks to the beat, then reads a poem the same way. The words have rhythm!

points.text: Rhythm is the beat you hear when you read a poem aloud
Some syllables are strong (BOOM), some soft (boom)
Rhythm makes poems fun to say and hear

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhythm is the drum inside the poem—tap along and feel it.

image.alt: Rhythm: The Heartbeat of Words — Poetry

slides.title: Feel the Rhythm
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads aloud and taps: 'The rain goes pit-ter-PAT-ter (tap tap TAP tap), On leaves of green and YEL-low.' Maya stamps her foot: she can feel the beat!

example.problem: Mark the strong beat (stress) in this line: 'The SNOW fell SOFT and WHITE and COLD'
example.solution: The SNOW fell SOFT and WHITE and COLD — every other syllable is stressed

slides.inSimpleWords: When you read a poem aloud, your body feels the rhythm.

slides.title: Simile: Comparing Two Things
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads: 'Her smile is bright like the sun.' Maya thinks: 'Oh! A smile is not really the sun, but it shines like the sun does. That's beautiful!'

points.text: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'
It helps us see something in a new, beautiful way
Examples: as strong as a tiger, bright like a star, soft as cotton

example.problem: Complete the simile: 'The river flows like _____' or 'Her voice is sweet as _____'
example.solution: The river flows like a snake. Her voice is sweet as honey.

slides.inSimpleWords: Similes are word pictures—they say 'this is like that' to show beauty.

image.alt: Simile: Comparing Two Things — Poetry

slides.title: Similes in Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Maya notices: 'Poet Uncle, my grandmother says I'm 'busy as a bee.' Is that a simile?' Poet Uncle nods proudly: 'Yes! You found one! People use similes all the time. Your mother might say you're 'good as gold' or 'stubborn as a mule.' Those are all similes hiding in regular talk!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Similes are everywhere—even in how people talk every day.

slides.title: Metaphor: One Thing IS Another
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads: 'Life is a journey.' Maya asks: 'But life isn't really a journey!' He smiles: 'In poetry, we can say life IS a journey because we grow and learn, just like travelers move ahead.'

points.text: A metaphor says one thing IS another (not 'like' another)
It makes us think deeply about the hidden meaning
Examples: 'Time is gold', 'Her heart is stone', 'Hope is a bird'

slides.inSimpleWords: Metaphors are magic—they make one thing become another in our minds.

image.alt: Metaphor: One Thing IS Another — Poetry

slides.title: Metaphor Magic
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle leans in: 'If I say 'Her heart is a stone,' I don't mean her heart is literally a rock. I mean she acts cold, hard to move, unfeeling. Metaphors take invisible feelings and give them shape. They make the invisible visible.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Metaphors transform feelings into things we can almost touch.

slides.title: A Poem About Rain
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads a complete poem for Maya:

example.problem: Read and find: (1) Rhyming words, (2) A simile, (3) The feeling of the poem.
example.solution:
Poem: 'Pitter-patter, pat-pat-pat, rain falls like a dancing cat. Splish and splash on the ground, nature's music is the sound. Wet and cold and fresh and free, rain brings joy to you and me.'

(1) pat/cat, ground/sound, free/me rhyme.
(2) Simile: 'rain falls like a dancing cat'
(3) Joy, playfulness, and love of nature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry shows us the beauty hiding in everyday things.

image.alt: A Poem About Rain — Poetry

slides.title: Write Your Own Poem
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives Maya a challenge: 'Write a short poem about something you love. It can be about your pet, your home, a friend, or nature. Use rhyming words and a simile if you can!'

example.problem: Write a 4-line poem about your favorite thing. Include at least one rhyme and one simile.
example.solution: My puppy is sweet like honey on bread, She plays with me from dawn till bed. Her eyes shine bright like stars so clear, I love my puppy, she's so dear!

slides.inSimpleWords: Poets are word artists—paint feelings, rhymes, and pictures on paper.

image.alt: Write Your Own Poem — Poetry

slides.title: Maya Finds Her Poet's Voice
slides.storyContext: By the end of class, Maya has written three poems—one about her mother's hands, one about the monsoon, one about her puppy. Poet Uncle reads them aloud with feeling. 'These are real poems,' he says. 'You have something to say, and you're saying it in the most beautiful way.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When you write a poem, you're speaking the language of the heart.

slides.title: Identify the Poetry Device
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shows Maya lines from different poems. Can she spot the rhyme, simile, metaphor, or rhythm?

example.problem:
What poetry device is in each line?
1. 'The sun danced across the sky'
2. 'Soft as silk and smooth as cream'
3. 'Rain falls pit-ter-PAT-ter, pit-ter-PAT-ter'
example.solution:
1. Metaphor (sun danced—sun doesn't really dance)
2. Simile (soft as, smooth as)
3. Rhythm (the beat is clear)

slides.inSimpleWords: Great poets know all the tricks—rhyme, rhythm, simile, metaphor.

slides.title: Poetry Lives in Your Heart
slides.storyContext: At the end of class, Poet Uncle sits with Maya and says: 'You don't need permission to write a poem. You just need a pencil and a feeling. A worry. A memory. A dream. A joy. Write about it in words that sing, and you're a poet.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Everyone is a poet—you just need to feel something and let words flow.

slides.title: More Poetry Devices: Alliteration and Sound

points.label: Alliteration
points.text: Repeating the same sound at the start of words: pretty pink petals

points.label: Onomatopoeia
points.text: Words that sound like their meaning: buzz, hiss, boom, splash

points.label: Repetition
points.text: Saying the same words over and over for effect

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry has many tricks—learn them all.

slides.title: Find the Devices
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shares examples of each device:

example.problem:
Spot the device in each line:
1. The bee buzzed busily by the big blue building
2. Crash! Bang! Boom! The thunder roared.
3. Never, never give up! Never, never stop dreaming!
example.solution:
1. Alliteration (B sound repeats)
2. Onomatopoeia (crash, bang, boom sound like the noise)
3. Repetition (never, never...repeats)

slides.inSimpleWords: Great poems use every trick in the book.

slides.title: Poets Are Dreamers
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle tells Maya: 'Poets see the world differently. They notice a spider web covered in dewdrops and see diamonds. They hear a child cry and feel the weight of the world. They love too much, dream too big, feel too deeply. That's why we read their poems—to feel alive.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poets are sensitive souls who share their hearts through words.

slides.title: Create a Poetry Slam Entry
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle invites students to write and perform poems for a class poetry slam—a celebration of student poets.

example.problem: Write a poem (any length) and be ready to read it aloud with feeling.
example.solution: Include: rhyme (at least 2 lines), rhythm (a beat you can tap), and one comparison (simile or metaphor). Most important: say something TRUE.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is for sharing—read it aloud and let others feel your words.

slides.title: Poems From India
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shares poems by Rabindranath Tagore, Sarojini Naidu, and other Indian poets. These poets wrote about nature, love, freedom, and India itself. Their words shaped a nation. Your words matter too.
slides.inSimpleWords: India has a rich poetry tradition—you are part of it.

slides.title: Poetry Journal
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives Maya a journal. Write one small poem every day for a week. About anything. Don't worry about perfect rhymes or rhythm. Just feel and write.

example.problem: Keep a poetry journal for 7 days. Topics: joy, sadness, nature, friendship, hope, fear, gratitude.
example.solution: Day 1 (joy): Ice cream melts, sweet and cold, a moment of pure happiness. Day 2 (sadness): Empty chair at the table, silence where laughter used to be.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry journals capture your feelings before they fade.

slides.title: Maya Becomes a Poet
slides.storyContext: By the end of the season, Maya has written 30 poems. Some are short, some long. Some rhyme, some don't. All of them are hers. She reads them to her parents, her friends, and her dog. They all listen, and they all feel something.
slides.inSimpleWords: You don't have to be famous to be a poet—you just have to feel.

slides.title: Write a Poem About Your Life
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. Write a poem about something important to you—a place, a person, a dream, or a feeling.

example.problem: Write a 4-8 line poem. Include: rhyme (at least 2 lines), one comparison (simile or metaphor), and rhythm (a beat).
example.solution: Example: My home is a fort of love (metaphor), Where laughter dances like fireflies (simile). My mother's arms wrap warm and soft, My father's jokes make my belly hurt with giggles (rhythm). This is my safe place (metaphor), This is where I belong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your life deserves a poem. Write it.

slides.title: Poetry is Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle's final lesson: Poetry isn't just in books. It's in your mother's prayers. It's in your grandmother's lullabies. It's in songs, prayers, and even in how people speak when they're heartbroken. Poetry is the language of the soul. You're a poet already—you just didn't know it.
slides.inSimpleWords: You are already a poet. Now own it.

slides.title: Poetry Magic

points.text: Rhyme makes poetry sound beautiful (words with the same ending sound)
Rhythm is the beat you feel when you read aloud
Similes compare using 'like' or 'as' (bright like a star)
Metaphors make one thing become another (life is a journey)
Poetry shows big feelings in small, beautiful words

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is the art of feeling with words—read it slowly, say it aloud, and let it touch your heart.

image.alt: Poetry Magic — Poetry

subject: Mathematics
title: Asha's Market Adventure: Counting to 1000
hook: Help Asha organize the fruit stall and learn how to count and write big numbers!

characters.name: Asha
characters.role: curious girl helping at her parents' fruit stall

slides.title: Numbers up to 1000
slides.storyContext: Asha is helping at her family's fruit stall in the morning market.

image.alt: Numbers up to 1000 — Numbers up to 1000

slides.title: The Fruit Stall Mystery
slides.storyContext: Papa says, 'Asha, count all our mangoes today!' There are so many! Asha starts counting: 1, 2, 3... but she loses track after 50. Her friend Ravi says, 'Let's make groups!' When they count 100 mangoes, Papa brings another basket with 100, then another. Now there are 300 mangoes! But how do we write 300 properly?

image.alt: The Fruit Stall Mystery — Numbers up to 1000

slides.title: Why Counting Big Numbers is Hard
slides.storyContext: Asha tries counting mangoes one by one: '1, 2, 3...' She gets to 50 and loses track. 'I forget where I was!' Ravi laughs. 'That's why we make groups. It's faster and easier!'

slides.title: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones
slides.storyContext: Ravi teaches Asha: 'We can break big numbers into groups. 100 is called ONE HUNDRED. Look—one group of 100 mangoes.'

points.label: 100 (one hundred)
points.text: one full group of 10 tens

points.label: 10 (one ten)
points.text: one group of 10 ones

points.label: 1 (one)
points.text: the smallest unit

example.problem: If we have 3 groups of 100 mangoes, how many mangoes in total?
example.solution: 3 × 100 = 300 mangoes

slides.inSimpleWords: A hundred is like 10 groups of 10. Three hundreds means 3 groups of 10 groups of 10.

slides.title: Breaking Down 300 Mangoes
slides.storyContext: Asha sees three big baskets of mangoes, each with 100. She writes on her clipboard: 100 + 100 + 100.

example.problem: How many mangoes in 3 baskets if each has 100?

slides.title: Adding More Mangoes to the Mix
slides.storyContext: Papa brings another batch! Now Asha has 300 mangoes from the three baskets, plus 5 more small groups of 10 mangoes (50 mangoes), plus 4 loose mangoes. 'Ravi, what's the total?' Ravi scratches his head and starts organizing.

slides.title: Writing Numbers: 347
slides.storyContext: Now Papa brings 3 more baskets of 100, and also 4 small groups of 10, and 7 loose mangoes. Asha writes the number carefully.

points.label: 3 Hundreds place
points.text: the number 3 in the 'hundreds' spot means 300

points.label: 4 Tens place
points.text: the number 4 in the 'tens' spot means 40

points.label: 7 Ones place
points.text: the number 7 in the 'ones' spot means 7

example.problem: Write: 300 + 40 + 7 as one number
example.solution: 347 (three hundred forty-seven)

slides.inSimpleWords: Each spot in a number tells you how many hundreds, tens, or ones there are. Left to right: biggest to smallest.

slides.title: Building 347 Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Asha lines up the mangoes: 3 big baskets (hundreds), 4 small bundles (tens), 7 single mangoes. She points to each group and says the number parts aloud.

example.problem: Show 347 as: ___ hundreds + ___ tens + ___ ones
example.solution: 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 7 ones = 347

slides.title: Expanded Form: What Every Digit Means
slides.storyContext: Ravi writes on the ground with chalk: 347 = 300 + 40 + 7. 'Each digit tells us a part of the whole number!'

points.label: Expanded form
points.text: breaks a number into its place-value parts

points.label: Each part has a name
points.text: hundreds, tens, ones

example.problem: Write 562 in expanded form

slides.inSimpleWords: Expanded form shows the value hiding inside each digit.

slides.title: Comparing Numbers: Which Stall Has More?
slides.storyContext: Next to Asha's stall is Meera's stall with 258 apples, and across is Vikram's stall with 385 apples. Who has more?

points.label: Compare hundreds first
points.text: 258 has 2 hundreds, 385 has 3 hundreds. 3 is bigger!

points.label: If hundreds are equal, compare tens
points.text: Look at the middle digit

points.label: If tens are equal, compare ones
points.text: Look at the last digit

example.problem: Compare 258 and 385. Which is bigger?
example.solution: 385 > 258 because 3 hundreds > 2 hundreds. Vikram's stall has more apples.

slides.inSimpleWords: To compare big numbers, look at the hundreds place first. The one with more hundreds is always bigger.

slides.title: Comparing Three Stalls
slides.storyContext: Asha now knows three fruit sellers: Meera (258), Vikram (385), and Suresh (312). She wants to order them by who has most fruit.

example.problem: Order 258, 385, and 312 from biggest to smallest
example.solution: 385 > 312 > 258 (Vikram has most, Meera has least)

slides.title: Ordering on the Number Line
slides.storyContext: Asha draws a number line to show all the stalls' fruit counts from smallest to biggest: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500...

points.label: Each number is 100 more
points.text: 400 is 100 more than 300

points.label: 1000 is the biggest!
points.text: one thousand = 10 groups of 100

slides.inSimpleWords: Skip counting by 100s helps us see patterns and order numbers quickly.

slides.title: Ravi's Skip-Counting Song
slides.storyContext: Ravi teaches Asha a rhythm: 'One hundred, two hundred, three hundred...' They clap as they count by 100s all the way to 1000. Papa laughs and joins in!

slides.title: Grouping by 10s and 1s
slides.storyContext: Asha now counts the oranges: she has 412 oranges. She counts: 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100, then 1 group of 100. Now 4 groups of 10 (that's 40). And 2 loose oranges.

points.label: 412 = 4 hundreds + 1 ten + 2 ones
points.text: 4 groups of 100 + 1 group of 10 + 2 loose

example.problem: Break 573 into hundreds, tens, and ones
example.solution: 5 hundreds (500) + 7 tens (70) + 3 ones (3) = 573

slides.inSimpleWords: Every number up to 1000 is just groups of 100, plus groups of 10, plus leftover ones.

slides.title: Decomposing 789
slides.storyContext: Papa has 789 bananas to sell. Asha breaks it down using baskets and loose bananas: 7 baskets of 100, 8 bundles of 10, and 9 single bananas.

example.problem: Write 789 as: ___ hundreds + ___ tens + ___ ones
example.solution: 7 hundreds + 8 tens + 9 ones = 789

slides.title: Representing Numbers on a Thousands Frame
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Asha a chart with boxes: 10 rows of 10 columns (100 squares per row, 1000 total). He shades some squares and says, 'This shows 347 out of 1000!'

points.label: A thousands frame has 1000 squares
points.text: 10 rows × 10 columns × 10 layers = 1000

points.label: Each row is 100 squares
points.text: Shade 3-and-a-half rows to show 347

points.label: See place value visually
points.text: Helps you understand what 347 looks like out of 1000

example.problem: Show 500 on a thousands frame. How many rows?
example.solution: 5 rows of 100 squares each = 500 squares shaded

slides.inSimpleWords: A thousands frame is like a visual map of numbers from 1 to 1000.

slides.title: The Big Count Challenge
slides.storyContext: At day's end, Asha counts the total sales. Papa sold 623 mangoes, Ravi helped count 178 bananas from another section. Asha wants to know: is 623 bigger than 178? Can she write 623 in words?

example.problem: Write 623 in words and tell: is 623 > 178? Why?
example.solution: 623 is 'six hundred twenty-three.' Yes, 623 > 178 because 6 hundreds > 1 hundred.

slides.title: Asha Counts Her Way to Success
slides.storyContext: By the end of the day, Asha has used numbers from 1 to 1000 many times! She confidently announces the totals to Papa, who is proud. 'My daughter is a mathematician!' he cheers.

slides.title: Reading and Writing Numbers in Words
slides.storyContext: Asha's friend Mali asks, 'How do you say 456?' Asha says carefully: 'Four hundred fifty-six.' Ravi writes it down: F-O-U-R H-U-N-D-R-E-D F-I-F-T-Y-S-I-X.

points.label: Say hundreds first
points.text: 456 → 'four hundred'

points.label: Then the tens and ones
points.text: 'fifty-six' (not 'fifty and six')

points.label: Practice: 789
points.text: 'seven hundred eighty-nine'

example.problem: Write these in words: 234, 501, 999
example.solution: Two hundred thirty-four, Five hundred one, Nine hundred ninety-nine

slides.inSimpleWords: Say the hundreds part, then the tens-and-ones part. Use a hyphen for twenty-one through ninety-nine.

slides.title: Number Ordering Challenge
slides.storyContext: Asha's cousin Priya brings four cards with numbers: 678, 543, 789, 601. Asha arranges them from smallest to largest using what she learned.

example.problem: Order 678, 543, 789, 601 from smallest to largest

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices something: 'When I count mangoes in pairs (2, 2, 2...), some numbers run out perfectly, and some have 1 left over!' Asha learns: even numbers divide evenly, odd numbers have 1 left.

points.label: Even numbers
points.text: Can be split into 2 equal groups: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10...

points.label: Odd numbers
points.text: Always have 1 left over: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9...

points.label: Look at the ones digit
points.text: Even ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Odd ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

example.problem: Is 347 even or odd? Is 500 even or odd?
example.solution: 347 is odd (ends in 7). 500 is even (ends in 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Check the last digit: even ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.

slides.title: Identifying Even and Odd from a Basket
slides.storyContext: Asha counts: 'Papa has 236 mangoes—that's even (ends in 6). Ravi has 145 bananas—that's odd (ends in 5).'

example.problem: List three even numbers between 100 and 1000
example.solution: Any three ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Example: 234, 567 is odd, 890 is even

slides.title: Your Turn: Sort the Inventory
slides.storyContext: Here are the counts from four fruit sellers on the same street: Stall A: 451 grapes, Stall B: 348 grapes, Stall C: 520 grapes, Stall D: 275 grapes. Arrange them from smallest to biggest!

example.problem: Order these: 451, 348, 520, 275 from smallest to biggest

slides.title: Challenge: Build Numbers from Digits
slides.storyContext: Asha has digit cards: 3, 5, 7. She wants to build the biggest number possible using all three. Ravi says, 'Put them in order from biggest to smallest!'

example.problem: Use digits 3, 5, 7 to make the biggest and smallest 3-digit numbers
example.solution: Biggest: 753. Smallest: 357

slides.title: Place Value in Action: 200 vs. 20 vs. 2
slides.storyContext: Asha realizes something amazing: the digit 2 can mean 2, or 20, or 200—depending on where it sits! She shows Ravi three numbers: 200, 20, 2.

points.label: 2 in the ones place
points.text: means just 2

points.label: 2 in the tens place
points.text: means 20 (ten times bigger!)

points.label: 2 in the hundreds place
points.text: means 200 (one hundred times bigger!)

example.problem: What does the 5 mean in each number: 5, 50, 500?
example.solution: 5 means 5. 50 means 5 tens. 500 means 5 hundreds.

slides.inSimpleWords: The position of a digit determines its true value.

slides.title: Decomposing Real Numbers from the Market
slides.storyContext: Papa brings a ledger showing daily sales: Tuesday 456 items, Wednesday 823 items, Thursday 539 items. Asha breaks each into place values for easy reading.

example.problem: Show 456, 823, 539 in expanded form

points.text: Numbers up to 1000 are made of hundreds, tens, and ones
Compare by looking at hundreds first, then tens, then ones
We can write numbers in expanded form (e.g., 347 = 300 + 40 + 7)
Skip counting by 100s helps us see patterns: 100, 200, 300...
Place value: the position of a digit determines its meaning
Every number can be read in words and written in standard form
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8; odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi's Cricket Tournament: Adding and Subtracting
hook: Ravi is organizing a cricket tournament. Learn addition and subtraction as he keeps score and counts players!

characters.name: Neha
characters.role: Ravi's friend who helps with scorekeeping

slides.title: Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Ravi is excited! His school is hosting a cricket tournament, and he's keeping the score.

image.alt: Addition and Subtraction — Addition and Subtraction

slides.title: Keeping Cricket Scores
slides.storyContext: On Day 1, Team Red scores 156 runs in the first innings. Coach Aman asks Ravi: 'If Team Blue scores 243 runs, do they win or lose?' Ravi scratches his head. 'I need to add and subtract big numbers!' Neha says, 'Let's line them up properly and use place values!'

slides.title: Why Ravi Needs Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Ravi realizes his job is tricky. He must add up runs across multiple innings and subtract penalties. 'This is real mathematics!' Coach Aman nods.

slides.title: Adding 1-Digit Numbers: The Basics
slides.storyContext: Ravi starts simple. First practice session: Team A gets 5 runs, then 3 more runs. Neha asks, 'How many total?'

points.text: Count on from 5: 6, 7, 8. Answer: 8

points.label: Use your fingers or objects
points.text: 5 fingers, add 3 more fingers

points.label: Say it aloud
points.text: 'Five plus three equals eight'

example.problem: A batter hits 7 runs. The next batter hits 4. Total?
example.solution: 7 + 4 = 11 runs

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding means putting groups together. Count on to find the answer.

slides.title: Quick Addition Practice
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: 6 + 2 = ? He counts on: 7, 8. Answer: 8. He's getting faster!

example.problem: Add these pairs: 3 + 4, 5 + 5, 2 + 7

slides.title: Subtracting 1-Digit Numbers: The Basics
slides.storyContext: Team Green had 9 runs but loses 4 runs due to a penalty. Ravi counts back on his fingers: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5. 'That's 5 left!'

points.text: Count back from 9: 8, 7, 6, 5. Answer: 5

points.label: Subtraction means taking away
points.text: Start at the bigger number, count back

points.label: Say it aloud
points.text: 'Nine minus four equals five'

example.problem: Team had 12 runs, lost 5. How many left?
example.solution: 12 - 5 = 7 runs remain

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction means taking away. Count back to find the answer.

slides.title: Adding 2-Digit Numbers: Ones First
slides.storyContext: First practice: Team A has 24 players, Team B brings 13 players. How many total? Ravi writes them in columns.

points.label: Line up ones and tens
points.text: 24 means 2 tens + 4 ones; 13 means 1 ten + 3 ones

points.label: Add the ones first
points.text: 4 + 3 = 7 ones

points.label: Add the tens next
points.text: 2 + 1 = 3 tens

points.label: Read the answer
points.text: 3 tens + 7 ones = 37

example.solution: 24 + 13 = 37 players total

slides.inSimpleWords: Line up the numbers by place value, add ones first, then tens.

slides.title: Adding More 2-Digit Numbers
slides.storyContext: Practice match scores: Team A scores 32 runs, Team B scores 45 runs. Ravi wants to know the combined total of both teams.

example.solution: Ones: 2 + 5 = 7. Tens: 3 + 4 = 7. Answer: 77 runs

slides.title: Subtracting 2-Digit Numbers: No Borrowing
slides.storyContext: Neha says, 'Team Green had 48 runs but lost 13 runs because of a penalty. How many are left?'

points.label: Line up by place value
points.text: Write 48 on top, 13 below

points.label: Subtract ones first
points.text: 8 - 3 = 5 ones

points.label: Subtract tens next
points.text: 4 - 1 = 3 tens

points.label: Answer: 35
points.text: 48 - 13 = 35 runs left

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction is taking away. Line up the numbers and subtract ones first, then tens.

slides.title: Subtracting More 2-Digit Numbers
slides.storyContext: Team Yellow had 67 runs from the first innings. In the second innings, they lost 24 runs due to mistakes. Ravi calculates.

example.solution: Ones: 7 - 4 = 3. Tens: 6 - 2 = 4. Answer: 43 runs

slides.title: Adding 3-Digit Numbers: Carrying Over
slides.storyContext: Now the real challenge! Team Red scored 156 runs in one match, Team Red scores 245 runs in another match. What's the total?

points.label: Add the ones: 6 + 5 = 11
points.text: 11 = 1 ten and 1 one. Write 1, carry 1 ten

points.label: Add the tens: 1 (carried) + 5 + 4 = 10
points.text: 10 tens = 1 hundred and 0 tens. Write 0, carry 1 hundred

points.label: Add the hundreds: 1 (carried) + 1 + 2 = 4
points.text: Write 4 hundreds

example.solution: 156 + 245 = 401 runs total

slides.inSimpleWords: When ones add up to 10 or more, that's a new ten! Move it to the tens place.

slides.title: Carrying Over in Action
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices more: 328 + 164. He carefully carries as ones and tens overflow into the next place value.

example.solution: Ones: 8 + 4 = 12 (write 2, carry 1). Tens: 2 + 6 + 1 = 9. Hundreds: 3 + 1 = 4. Answer: 492

slides.title: Subtracting with Borrowing
slides.storyContext: Coach Aman asks: 'Team Blue had 332 runs. They lost 147 runs in a mistake. How many left?'

points.label: Look at ones: 2 - 7. Can't do it!
points.text: Borrow 1 ten from the tens place

points.label: Now ones: 12 - 7 = 5 ones
points.text: We turned 1 ten into 10 ones

points.label: Tens: 2 tens (left after borrowing) - 4 tens. Can't do it!
points.text: Borrow 1 hundred

points.label: Now tens: 12 - 4 = 8 tens
points.text: And hundreds: 2 - 1 = 1

example.solution: Borrow and regroup. 332 - 147 = 185 runs

slides.inSimpleWords: When you can't subtract, borrow from the next place value (like borrowing money from a friend!)

slides.title: Borrowing in Action
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: 423 - 156. His ones digit is too small, so he borrows. He gets 267 as the answer.

example.solution: Ones: can't do 3 - 6, borrow → 13 - 6 = 7. Tens: can't do 1 - 5, borrow → 11 - 5 = 6. Hundreds: 3 - 1 = 2. Answer: 267

slides.title: Word Problems: Adding Runs Across Innings
slides.storyContext: Team Yellow scored 123 runs in the first innings, 156 runs in the second, and 87 runs in the third. Total?

points.label: Check your work
points.text: Does 366 make sense?

slides.inSimpleWords: To add more than two numbers, add the first two, then add the third to that answer.

slides.title: Tournament Final Score
slides.storyContext: Final match! Team Red (467 runs) vs Team Blue (389 runs). By how many runs does Red win?

example.problem: Find the difference: 467 - 389
example.solution: 467 - 389 = 78. Team Red wins by 78 runs!

slides.title: Ravi Becomes the Tournament Hero
slides.storyContext: By tournament's end, Ravi has added and subtracted hundreds of scores. Coach Aman hugs him: 'You kept perfect records! This is real mathematics in action!'

slides.title: Fact Families: Related Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Neha discovers something cool: if 3 + 5 = 8, then 5 + 3 = 8, and 8 - 3 = 5, and 8 - 5 = 3. They all connect!

points.label: Addition is commutative
points.text: 3 + 5 = 8 and 5 + 3 = 8 (same answer!)

points.label: Subtraction undoes addition
points.text: 8 - 3 = 5 is the 'opposite' of 3 + 5 = 8

example.problem: Write all fact families for 4, 6, and 10

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition and subtraction are opposites. They always come in related groups.

slides.title: Using Fact Families to Check Answers
slides.storyContext: Ravi adds 47 + 23 = 70. To check, he subtracts: 70 - 23 should equal 47. It does! He's confident in his answer.

example.problem: Check: 156 + 245 = 401 using subtraction
example.solution: 401 - 156 should equal 245. Check: 401 - 156 = 245. Correct!

slides.title: Missing Number Problems
slides.storyContext: Coach asks Ravi: 'Team A scored some runs, Team B scored 34 more, and together they scored 127. How many did Team A score?'

example.problem: What number plus 45 equals 120?

slides.inSimpleWords: Work backwards using subtraction to find missing numbers.

slides.title: Your Turn: Cricket Tournament Math
slides.storyContext: Three teams' scores: Team A: 234 runs, Team B: 156 runs, Team C: 289 runs. (a) How many more runs does C have than B? (b) What's the total of all three teams?

example.solution: (a) 289 - 156 = 133 runs more for C. (b) 234 + 156 + 289 = 679 runs total

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Tournament Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Team Red scored 345 runs in Match 1 and 267 runs in Match 2. Team Blue scored 412 runs in Match 1 and 298 runs in Match 2. Which team scored more total? By how much?

example.problem: Red total: 345 + 267. Blue total: 412 + 298. Find the difference.

slides.title: Ravi's Scorecard Blues
slides.storyContext: Day 2: Ravi adds 234 + 156 + 189 (scores across three matches). He realizes: 'This is getting complex! I need a system.'

slides.title: Grouping Numbers for Easier Calculation
slides.storyContext: Coach Aman shows Ravi: 'Instead of adding 3 big numbers at once, add the first two, then add the third to the result.'

example.problem: Add 112 + 225 + 143 step-by-step

slides.inSimpleWords: Break big addition into smaller chunks. Add two, then add the third.

slides.title: Verifying Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Ravi checks: Team A (123 + 167 + 145). He calculates step by step and double-checks using fact families.

slides.title: Zero in Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Neha asks: 'What if a team scores 0 runs in an innings?' Ravi learns: 'Zero means nothing was added. The total stays the same.'

points.label: Adding zero
points.text: 52 + 0 = 52 (adding nothing changes nothing)

points.label: Subtracting zero
points.text: 52 - 0 = 52 (taking away nothing leaves everything)

points.label: Zero as the first number
points.text: 0 + 45 = 45 (starting from nothing, then adding 45)

slides.inSimpleWords: Zero doesn't change the answer. Adding or subtracting zero keeps the number the same.

points.text: Always line up numbers by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens)
For addition: add ones first, then tens, then hundreds
When ones add to 10+, carry a ten to the tens place
For subtraction: subtract ones first, then tens, then hundreds
If you can't subtract, borrow from the next place value
Word problems: read carefully, decide if you add or subtract, then solve
Addition and subtraction are opposites (fact families)
Use subtraction to check your addition, and vice versa

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Garden Project: Learning Measurement
hook: Priya is growing a garden at home. Learn how to measure length, weight, and capacity!

characters.name: Grandma
characters.role: wise grandmother who teaches traditional measures

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Priya's cousin who helps with the garden

slides.title: Measurement
slides.storyContext: Priya starts a vegetable garden in her backyard. She needs to measure everything!

slides.title: Growing a Garden
slides.storyContext: Grandma says, 'Priya, to grow sunflowers, you need to know how tall they'll get. And tomatoes need a pot that holds enough water.' Arjun asks, 'How do we measure?' Grandma brings out a ruler, a weighing scale, and a water jug. 'These are our tools!'

slides.title: Why Measurement Matters in Gardening
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: 'If I don't know the height of the garden fence, I can't plant tall sunflowers there. If I don't track the water, my plants die!' Measurement is essential.

slides.title: What is Measurement?
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'How do we know if something is big or small, heavy or light, full or empty?' Grandma explains: 'We use measurement to compare things.'

points.label: Measurement compares
points.text: Measures show how much of something we have

points.label: We measure three things
points.text: Length (how long), Weight (how heavy), Capacity (how much liquid)

points.label: We use tools and units
points.text: Rulers, scales, and jugs measure in centimeters, grams, and liters

example.problem: What do we measure to find: (a) if a stick is long? (b) if a bag is heavy? (c) if a bottle is full?
example.solution: (a) Length (b) Weight (c) Capacity

slides.inSimpleWords: Measurement tells us how big, how heavy, or how full something is.

slides.title: Measuring Length: Centimeters and Meters
slides.storyContext: Priya's sunflower seedling is tiny. 'How tall is it?' She uses a ruler marked in centimeters (cm).

points.label: Centimeter (cm)
points.text: a small unit. A fingernail is about 1 cm wide

points.label: Meter (m)
points.text: a bigger unit. 100 cm = 1 meter (about the height of a door)

points.label: Measure carefully
points.text: Line the ruler at the zero mark and read where it ends

example.problem: Priya's seedling is 12 cm tall today. In 2 weeks, it's 34 cm. How much did it grow?
example.solution: 34 - 12 = 22 cm of growth

slides.inSimpleWords: Centimeters measure small things (fingers, seeds), meters measure bigger things (doors, gardens).

slides.title: Measuring Garden Plants
slides.storyContext: Priya measures her growing plants weekly: Week 1 tomato is 8 cm, Week 2 it's 15 cm, Week 3 it's 23 cm. She tracks the changes.

example.problem: How much did the tomato grow from Week 1 to Week 3?
example.solution: 23 - 8 = 15 cm of growth

slides.title: Comparing Lengths
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows carrots. His longest carrot is 18 cm. Priya's longest is 15 cm. 'Who grew the longer carrot?'

points.label: Compare two lengths
points.text: 18 cm > 15 cm. Arjun's is longer

points.label: The difference
points.text: 18 - 15 = 3 cm longer

points.label: Order from shortest to longest
points.text: Use comparison symbols: <, >, =

example.problem: Arjun's carrot: 18 cm, Priya's: 15 cm. Order from shortest to longest.
example.solution: 15 cm < 18 cm. Priya's is shorter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare by measuring both and seeing which number is bigger.

slides.title: Measuring Weight: Kilograms and Grams
slides.storyContext: Priya picks her first tomato! 'How heavy is it?' Grandma puts it on a weighing scale.

points.label: Gram (g)
points.text: a tiny unit. A paperclip weighs about 1 gram

points.label: Kilogram (kg)
points.text: a heavy unit. 1000 grams = 1 kilogram (like a big bag of rice)

points.label: Scale shows weight
points.text: Read the number where the needle stops

example.problem: One tomato weighs 120 grams. Priya picks 5 tomatoes of the same weight. Total weight?
example.solution: 120 × 5 = 600 grams (or just under 1 kilogram)

slides.inSimpleWords: Grams measure light things, kilograms measure heavy things like food at the market.

slides.title: Weighing Garden Produce
slides.storyContext: Priya harvests vegetables: tomato 150 g, carrot 120 g, eggplant 180 g. She weighs each and records the amounts.

example.problem: Total weight of all three vegetables?
example.solution: 150 + 120 + 180 = 450 grams (about half a kilogram)

slides.title: Measuring Capacity: Liters and Milliliters
slides.storyContext: Every morning, Priya waters her plants. Grandma gives her a water jug. 'This jug holds 1 liter. How much water does the garden need?'

points.label: Milliliter (mL)
points.text: a small amount. A teaspoon holds about 5 mL

points.label: Liter (L)
points.text: a bigger amount. 1000 mL = 1 liter (like a water bottle)

points.label: Measure with a jug
points.text: Pour carefully and read the markings on the side

example.problem: Priya waters 8 plants, using 2 liters per plant. How much water total?
example.solution: 8 × 2 = 16 liters of water used

slides.inSimpleWords: Milliliters are for tiny amounts (medicine, juice), liters are for bigger amounts (water, milk).

slides.title: Watering the Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya's garden has 5 tomato pots, 3 carrot pots, and 2 herb pots. Each pot needs 1 liter of water. How much water in total?

example.problem: Total pots: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 pots. Water needed?
example.solution: 10 pots × 1 liter = 10 liters of water total

slides.title: Comparing and Adding Measurements
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows carrots. His longest carrot is 18 cm. Priya's longest is 15 cm. 'Let's put them together in a line!'

points.label: Compare two measurements
points.text: 18 cm > 15 cm. Arjun's is longer

points.label: Add measurements
points.text: 18 + 15 = 33 cm if lined end-to-end

points.label: Subtract measurements
points.text: 18 - 15 = 3 cm. Arjun's is 3 cm longer

example.problem: Add these lengths: 25 cm + 34 cm + 18 cm = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: You can add and subtract measurements just like regular numbers!

slides.title: Time and Growth: Days and Weeks
slides.storyContext: Priya keeps a garden diary. 'My tomato plant was 10 cm on Day 1. Now it's Day 21, and it's 45 cm. How much grew each week?'

points.label: Measure growth over time
points.text: Record height on Day 1, Day 8, Day 15, Day 22

points.label: Calculate week-by-week growth
points.text: Subtract to find the difference

points.label: Compare weeks
points.text: Which week had the most growth?

example.problem: Day 1: 10 cm, Day 8: 18 cm, Day 15: 32 cm, Day 22: 45 cm. Growth in Week 2?
example.solution: Week 2 growth: 32 - 18 = 14 cm

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure over time to see how fast plants grow. Subtraction shows you the change!

slides.title: Tracking Plant Growth Chart
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a chart of her sunflower's height: Week 1: 5 cm, Week 2: 12 cm, Week 3: 22 cm, Week 4: 35 cm. She notices it grows faster each week!

example.problem: Which week had the most growth? Week 1→2, 2→3, or 3→4?
example.solution: Week 1→2: 7 cm. Week 2→3: 10 cm. Week 3→4: 13 cm. Week 3→4 had most growth!

slides.title: Converting Between Units
slides.storyContext: Grandma says: 'If your plant is 100 cm tall, that's 1 meter. If you harvest 2 kilograms of tomatoes, that's 2000 grams!'

points.label: 100 centimeters = 1 meter
points.text: Bigger unit, fewer of them needed

points.label: 1000 grams = 1 kilogram
points.text: Smaller units make bigger measurements

points.label: 1000 milliliters = 1 liter
points.text: Convert by multiplying or dividing by 1000

example.problem: Priya's carrot is 20 cm. How much shorter than 1 meter?
example.solution: 1 meter = 100 cm. 100 - 20 = 80 cm shorter than 1 meter

slides.inSimpleWords: Big units and small units measure the same thing differently.

slides.title: Converting Real Garden Measurements
slides.storyContext: Priya measures her sunflower: 156 cm tall. 'Is that more than 1 meter?' She calculates: 156 cm = 1 meter 56 cm, or 1.56 meters.

example.problem: Convert: 156 cm = ? meters and ? cm
example.solution: 156 cm = 1 meter + 56 cm = 1 m 56 cm

slides.title: The Garden Harvest Report
slides.storyContext: End of the season! Priya reports: Sunflower height: 187 cm. Tomatoes harvested: 12 kg total. Water used: 240 liters. What was her biggest plant?

example.problem: Compare plant height: Sunflower 187 cm vs. Grandma's record sunflower 156 cm. How much taller?
example.solution: 187 - 156 = 31 cm. Priya's sunflower is 31 cm taller!

slides.title: Priya Wins the Garden Contest
slides.storyContext: The school's 'Best Garden' competition measures all student gardens by height of tallest plant, total harvest weight, and efficiency of water use. Priya's measurements show her garden is a winner!

slides.title: Estimating Measurements
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at a plant and guesses: 'This is about 15 cm tall.' Then he measures: 14 cm. 'My estimate was close!' Grandma says: 'Estimation helps us know if our real measurement makes sense.'

points.label: Estimate first
points.text: Make a reasonable guess using what you know

points.label: Then measure
points.text: Use a ruler, scale, or jug to get the exact number

points.label: Compare
points.text: Is your estimate close to the real number?

example.problem: Estimate: Is a tomato heavier than 100 grams? Then weigh it.
example.solution: Estimate: yes, probably. Real: 120 grams. Estimate was close!

slides.inSimpleWords: Good estimators are ready for the real measurement.

slides.title: Practice Estimation in the Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya guesses: 'That watermelon looks like 3 kg.' She weighs it: 2.8 kg. 'Very close!'

example.problem: Estimate the height of a tomato plant, then measure
example.solution: Estimate: 30 cm. Actual: 32 cm. Good estimate!

slides.title: Your Turn: Measure Your Garden
slides.storyContext: You have three plants: Plant A is 24 cm tall and weighs 150 grams. Plant B is 35 cm tall and weighs 280 grams. Plant C is 18 cm tall and weighs 95 grams. (a) Which plant is tallest? (b) What's the total height? (c) Which plant weighs the most?

example.problem: (a) Compare heights: 24, 35, 18. (b) Add all heights. (c) Compare weights: 150, 280, 95.
example.solution: (a) Plant B at 35 cm. (b) 24 + 35 + 18 = 77 cm total. (c) Plant B at 280 grams

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-Step Measurement Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya's garden uses 20 liters of water per day for 7 days. Her plants gain a total of 5 kg of weight from all the growth. How much water used? How many grams of growth?

example.problem: (a) 20 liters × 7 days = ? (b) 5 kg = ? grams
example.solution: (a) 140 liters of water. (b) 5 × 1000 = 5000 grams of growth

slides.title: Comparing Measurements Across Units
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'My plant is 1 meter 20 centimeters. Priya's is 95 centimeters. Whose is taller?' Priya converts to compare.

points.label: Compare
points.text: 120 cm > 95 cm

example.problem: Compare: 1 meter 50 cm vs 145 cm

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert big units to small units, then compare the numbers.

slides.title: Real-World Unit Conversion: Harvest Day
slides.storyContext: Priya harvested 2 kg of tomatoes, 800 g of carrots, and 1 kg 200 g of peppers. She wants the total in kilograms.

example.problem: Convert and add: 2 kg + 800 g + (1 kg 200 g)
example.solution: 2 kg + 0.8 kg + 1.2 kg = 4 kg total

slides.title: Practical Measurement: Planting Spacing
slides.storyContext: Grandma teaches: 'Tomato plants need 30 cm between them. If you have 4 plants in a row, how much space total?'

points.label: Distance between plants
points.text: 30 cm is the standard spacing

points.label: Calculate total spacing
points.text: 4 plants need 3 gaps: 3 × 30 = 90 cm

points.label: Add extra for edges
points.text: Plus space at the start and end

example.problem: 5 plants with 25 cm spacing between them. Space needed?
example.solution: 4 gaps × 25 cm = 100 cm (plus edge space)

slides.inSimpleWords: Real gardening uses measurement for layout and spacing.

points.text: Length is measured in centimeters (cm) and meters (m). 100 cm = 1 meter
Weight is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1000 g = 1 kg
Capacity (how much liquid) is measured in milliliters (mL) and liters (L). 1000 mL = 1 L
You can add and subtract measurements like regular numbers
Measure the same thing over time to see how it changes
Different tools: ruler for length, scale for weight, jug for capacity
Estimate before measuring to check if your answer makes sense
Big units (m, kg, L) and small units (cm, g, mL) measure the same things differently

subject: Mathematics
title: Vikram's Tile Shop: Exploring Shapes
hook: Vikram's family owns a tile shop. Learn about shapes, angles, and symmetry through colorful patterns!

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: boy learning about shapes in his family's tile shop

characters.name: Papa
characters.role: tile shop owner who knows shapes and patterns

characters.name: Divya
characters.role: Vikram's classmate who loves art and design

slides.title: Geometry
slides.storyContext: Vikram helps arrange tiles in his father's shop and discovers beautiful shapes and patterns.

slides.title: The Tile Shop Mystery
slides.storyContext: Papa says, 'Vikram, these tiles aren't just square! Look—some are triangles, some are circles. And these patterns! See the symmetry?' Divya visits and says, 'I love the hexagon tiles! They fit perfectly together.' Vikram wonders: 'How do all these shapes fit together? What makes them special?'

slides.title: Vikram Sorts the Tiles
slides.storyContext: Papa asks Vikram to organize new tiles by shape. 'Put all the pointy ones here, the smooth round ones there,' he says. Vikram moves slowly, touching each tile, noticing differences. Some tiles feel sharp at the corners, others smooth all around. He stacks them by category.

points.text: Different shapes have different looks and feels.
Sorting by shape helps us understand what makes each special.

slides.title: 2D Shapes: Sides and Vertices
slides.storyContext: Papa shows Vikram different flat tiles and they count the corners (vertices) and edges (sides).

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 sides, 3 corners (vertices)

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 4 corners

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: 4 sides (opposite sides equal), 4 right angles, 4 corners

points.label: Circle
points.text: No sides, no corners, perfectly round

example.problem: Papa shows a hexagon tile. How many sides and corners does it have?
example.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes are made of straight sides and pointy corners, except circles which are smooth and round.

slides.title: Counting Sides: Triangles vs Squares
slides.storyContext: Vikram picks up a triangular tile and a square tile. Papa asks him to count and compare.

example.problem: A triangle has 3 sides. A square has 4 sides. How many more sides does a square have?
example.solution: 4 - 3 = 1. A square has 1 more side than a triangle.

points.text: Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners
Square: 4 sides, 4 corners
More sides = shape gets more corners too

slides.title: Right Angles and Corners
slides.storyContext: Vikram learns that some corners in shapes are special. Papa says, 'These tiles have four right angles. See? They fit perfectly into the wall!'

points.label: Right angle (90°)
points.text: a perfect corner, like the corner of a book or the edge of a square

points.label: Squares and rectangles
points.text: have four right angles

points.label: Triangles
points.text: may have one, or no right angles

points.label: Check with a square tool
points.text: A small square corner can test if angles are right

example.problem: Does a triangle always have a right angle?
example.solution: No. Some triangles have one right angle, some have none. The sum of all angles in a triangle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: A right angle is a corner that is exactly square, like the corner of a cardboard box.

slides.title: Divya's Corner Test
slides.storyContext: Divya brings a small cardboard square corner from art class. She tests tiles with it. 'This rectangle fits perfectly—four right angles!' she says. She tries it on a triangle tile. 'Only one corner is right.' She tries on a circle. 'No corners at all!'

points.text: Different shapes have different numbers of right angles.
We can test angles using a simple square tool.

slides.title: Line Symmetry: Mirror Images
slides.storyContext: Divya draws a line down the middle of a tile and says, 'Look! If I fold here, both sides match perfectly. That's symmetry!'

points.label: Symmetry
points.text: when both sides of a line are exactly the same

points.label: Line of symmetry
points.text: the imaginary line where you fold

points.label: Examples
points.text: square has 4 lines, rectangle has 2, triangle may have 1 or 0

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? A triangle?
example.solution: Square: 4 lines. Triangle: 1 line (only if it's isosceles), 0 lines (if it's scalene).

slides.inSimpleWords: A shape has symmetry if you can fold it and both sides match exactly.

slides.title: Finding Symmetry in Tiles
slides.storyContext: Vikram folds paper copies of different tiles to find their lines of symmetry.

example.problem: Fold a square tile in half. Do both halves match? Now fold it corner-to-corner. Do they match? How many ways can you fold a square so both sides match?
example.solution: A square matches when folded 4 ways: vertically, horizontally, and diagonally (twice). A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

points.text: Squares have 4 lines of symmetry.
Rectangles have 2 lines of symmetry.
Some triangles have 1, some have none.

slides.title: 3D Shapes: Cubes and Cuboids
slides.storyContext: Papa pulls out a tile display box (a cube). 'This is a 3D shape! It has faces (the flat sides), edges (the lines where faces meet), and vertices (the corners).'

points.label: Cube
points.text: 6 square faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices (vertices are called corners in everyday language)

points.label: Cuboid (rectangular box)
points.text: 6 rectangular faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices

points.label: Sphere (ball)
points.text: no faces, no edges, no vertices. Perfectly round in all directions

example.problem: How many faces, edges, and vertices does a cube have?
example.solution: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes have flat faces, lines where faces meet (edges), and pointy corners (vertices).

slides.title: Vikram Builds with 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Papa gives Vikram wooden blocks—cubes and cuboids. Vikram stacks them and touches the edges and corners. 'Each corner is like where three walls meet in a room!' he discovers. Papa smiles and corrects: 'That corner is called a vertex.'

points.text: 3D shapes are solid and take up space.
We can count faces, edges, and vertices on 3D shapes.

slides.title: Counting Parts of a Cuboid
slides.storyContext: Vikram's tile display box is a cuboid. He carefully traces and counts each part.

example.problem: Vikram's tile box is shaped like a cuboid (rectangular prism). Count its faces, edges, and vertices.
example.solution: Cuboid: 6 faces (rectangles on all sides), 12 edges (lines where two faces meet), 8 vertices (corners where three faces meet).

points.text: Opposite faces are equal in a cuboid.
Every edge connects two vertices.
Every vertex is where three edges meet.

slides.title: Patterns and Tiling
slides.storyContext: Vikram arranges small tiles into a pattern. Some tiles repeat in rows. Some fit together with no gaps (like hexagons!). Divya says, 'This is tessellation—the shapes tile perfectly!'

points.label: Repeating pattern
points.text: Shapes follow a rule. Example: square, triangle, square, triangle...

points.label: Tessellation
points.text: Shapes fit together with no gaps or overlaps

points.label: Examples
points.text: Squares, rectangles, and hexagons tessellate. Circles don't (they leave gaps)

example.problem: If you tile a floor with only hexagons, will there be gaps?
example.solution: No. Hexagons tessellate perfectly—they fit together with no gaps.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes fit together perfectly to cover a floor with no spaces. Others leave gaps.

slides.title: Designing Vikram's Floor
slides.storyContext: Vikram and Papa plan a new tile floor for the shop entrance. 'We need a pattern that looks beautiful and fits perfectly,' Papa says. Vikram sketches squares and triangles arranged in rows. 'Will they tessellate?' Vikram wonders aloud.

points.text: Designers choose shapes that tessellate well.
Patterns can follow rules like: repeat every 4 tiles, alternate colors, etc.

slides.title: Designing a Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Vikram designs a new floor pattern. He uses squares and triangles. Each square has a triangle on top and bottom. How many triangles does he need for 10 squares?

example.problem: Pattern: 1 square needs 2 triangles (one on top, one on bottom). For 10 squares, how many triangles?
example.solution: 10 × 2 = 20 triangles needed.

slides.title: A Hexagon Discovery
slides.storyContext: Divya brings a picture of a honeycomb to the tile shop. 'Look! Bees make perfect hexagons!' Vikram is amazed. Papa explains: 'Hexagons are nature's favorite shape for fitting perfectly. They appear in honeycombs, flower petals, and soccer balls!'

points.text: Hexagons appear in nature and are efficient shapes.
Six-sided shapes fit together without gaps.

slides.title: Why Shapes Matter in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Papa shows Vikram how shapes are everywhere in the tile shop and beyond.

points.text: Shapes are the foundation of geometry and design.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding shapes helps us build things, appreciate nature, and create beautiful designs.

slides.title: Your Turn: Shape Detective
slides.storyContext: Look at these 2D shapes: A—triangle with all sides equal, B—rectangle, C—circle. (a) Which have right angles? (b) Which have lines of symmetry? (c) If you arrange B in a row, do they tessellate?

example.problem: (a) Which shapes have right angles? (b) How many lines of symmetry does each? (c) Do rectangles tessellate?
example.solution: (a) Rectangle (B) and circle are special; triangle depends on type. (b) Triangle: 1 (or 0), Rectangle: 2, Circle: infinite. (c) Yes, rectangles tessellate perfectly.

image.alt: Your Turn: Shape Detective — Geometry

slides.title: Challenge: Design Your Own Tessellation
slides.storyContext: Vikram is challenged to design a floor pattern using only one type of shape that tessellates perfectly.

example.problem: Choose ONE shape (square, rectangle, or hexagon) and design a pattern that covers a 4×4 grid with no gaps or overlaps. Can you color alternating shapes in two colors?
example.solution: If using squares: arrange in a 4×4 grid (16 squares total). Color alternating squares red and blue like a checkerboard. All gaps are filled, no overlaps. Pattern is balanced and pretty.

points.text: Squares, rectangles, and hexagons all tessellate.
Tessellations can be colored to create patterns.

slides.title: Shapes in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Divya brings pictures of famous buildings: the Taj Mahal (domes and symmetry), temples (triangular roofs), modern offices (rectangles and glass cubes). Vikram realizes: 'All buildings are made of shapes!' Papa nods. 'Architects use shapes to make buildings strong and beautiful.'

points.text: Real buildings use geometry to stand strong.
Symmetry appears in famous architecture worldwide.

slides.title: Shapes in Nature
slides.storyContext: Vikram finds shapes in nature: spider web hexagons, snowflake symmetry, sunflower spiral seeds, honeycomb perfection. 'Nature uses geometry too!' he exclaims. Papa smiles. 'Nature invented geometry millions of years before humans. Every shape has a purpose—efficient, strong, and beautiful.'

points.text: Nature uses perfect geometry for efficiency and beauty.
Shapes appear everywhere in the natural world.

slides.title: Angles in Everyday Objects
slides.storyContext: Vikram finds right angles in the tile shop and beyond.

example.problem: Look around: door frame (4 right angles), book corner (4 right angles), picture frame (4 right angles), pencil point (acute angle), open door (variable angles). How many right angles can you count in this room?
example.solution: Corners of windows, doors, tiles, shelves, tables all have right angles. Most human-made objects use right angles for stability and practicality. Acute angles (less than 90°) are used in roofs and arrows for efficiency.

points.text: Right angles appear everywhere in human design.
Different angles serve different purposes.

slides.title: Vikram Becomes a Tile Master
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Vikram can identify shapes, count sides and corners, find lines of symmetry, and design patterns. Papa is proud. 'You've learned geometry through tiles,' he says. Vikram grins: 'Now I see shapes everywhere!'

points.text: Vikram mastered 2D and 3D shapes, angles, symmetry, and tessellation.
Understanding shapes makes the world more interesting.

slides.title: Transformations - Moving Shapes
slides.storyContext: Divya shows Vikram three ways to move shapes: slide, flip, turn.

points.text: Transformations help us create patterns and designs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes can slide, flip, and turn but remain the same shape—just in different positions.

slides.title: Shapes Around You
slides.storyContext: Vikram realizes geometry isn't just in the tile shop. It's in sports (soccer ball spheres), clothing (symmetrical designs), food (circular pizzas, triangular chips), games (dice cubes), and art. 'Every part of the world uses shapes,' he tells Divya. 'We just need to learn to see them.'

points.text: Geometry is everywhere in daily life.
Learning geometry helps you see the world more deeply.
2D shapes are flat: triangles (3 sides), squares/rectangles (4 sides), circles (no sides)
Squares and rectangles have four right angles (90° corners)
Symmetry means a shape's two sides match when folded
3D shapes have faces (flat sides), edges (lines), and vertices (corners)
Cubes and cuboids are common 3D shapes in real life (boxes, dice)
Some shapes tessellate (fit together perfectly) like squares and hexagons
