subject: Science
title: Asha's Garden Discovery
hook: Learn how plants grow and what each part does!

slides.title: Plants - Parts and Functions
slides.storyContext: Asha visits her grandpa's garden in Punjab and discovers how plants work.

image.alt: Plants - Parts and Functions — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: In Grandpa's Garden
slides.storyContext: Asha sees vegetables, fruit trees, and flowers. Grandpa asks: 'Do you know why plants have roots, stems, leaves, and flowers?' Asha shakes her head. 'Then let's explore together,' he smiles.

image.alt: In Grandpa's Garden — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Digging Deep
slides.storyContext: Grandpa and Asha carefully dig near a spinach plant. As they pull the plant gently, long white thread-like parts come out of the soil. 'Those are roots!' Grandpa says excitedly. Asha is amazed. 'There are so many tiny ones!' She touches them—they're wet and cool.

points.text: Roots grow underground and are hidden from sight.
Roots absorb water and stay connected to soil.

slides.title: Roots - The Hidden Workers
slides.storyContext: Grandpa digs gently near a tomato plant and shows Asha the roots hidden below the soil.

points.label: What are roots?
points.text: Roots are parts of the plant that grow underground.

points.label: What do they do?
points.text: Roots drink water and nutrients from the soil.

points.label: They also hold
points.text: Roots keep the plant firmly in the ground so it doesn't fall over.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots are like a plant's drinking straw and anchor.

image.alt: Roots - The Hidden Workers — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: The Root Test
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Asha two plants: one in wet soil, one in dry soil.

example.problem: Grandpa has two identical plants. One is planted in moist soil with strong roots. One is planted in dry soil. After one week, which plant looks healthier?
example.solution: The plant in moist soil is healthier because its roots can absorb water and nutrients. The dry soil plant may wilt because its roots can't find enough water.

points.text: Roots need water in soil to keep plants alive.
Dry soil = weak roots = weak plant.

slides.title: Stems - The Plant's Backbone
slides.storyContext: Asha holds a stick from the mango tree. Grandpa says: 'That's what a stem looks like inside.'

points.label: What is a stem?
points.text: The stem is the main part that grows upward from the ground.

points.label: It carries water
points.text: Water from roots travels up the stem to leaves and flowers.

points.label: It supports
points.text: The stem holds leaves, flowers, and fruits high up in the air.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stem is like the plant's backbone and water pipe.

image.alt: Stems - The Plant's Backbone — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Tracking Water Through the Stem
slides.storyContext: Grandpa cuts a fresh stem in half. 'See these tiny tubes inside?' He shows Asha the cross-section. 'Water travels up through these like a highway.' He breaks a thin stem and shows her how water trickles out. 'The stem is like thousands of drinking straws bundled together!'

points.text: Stems contain tiny tubes that transport water.
Water travels from roots through the stem to every leaf.

slides.title: Leaves - The Plant's Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Asha touches a mango leaf and looks at the veins running through it. 'What are these lines?' she asks.

points.label: What are leaves?
points.text: Leaves are flat, green parts that grow on the stem.

points.label: They make food
points.text: Leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food for the plant.

points.label: Veins in leaves
points.text: The lines carry water and food inside the leaf, like roads for nutrients.

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves are the plant's kitchen where it makes food from sunlight.

image.alt: Leaves - The Plant's Kitchen — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Why Leaves Are Green
slides.storyContext: Asha asks Grandpa a big question.

example.problem: Why are leaves green and not red or yellow like some flowers?
example.solution: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a special pigment that captures sunlight. Green is best at absorbing light energy for making food. Some leaves turn red or yellow in autumn when they stop making food.

points.text: Green color = special chemical for capturing sunlight.
Sunlight + water + air in leaves = plant food (glucose).

slides.title: Flowers - The Plant's Gift
slides.storyContext: A bright red chili flower catches Asha's eye. Grandpa grins. 'This flower will become a chili pepper!'

points.label: What are flowers?
points.text: Flowers are beautiful, colorful parts of the plant.

points.label: They make seeds
points.text: After flowers are pollinated, they grow into fruits and seeds.

points.label: They attract
points.text: Bright colors and smells attract bees and butterflies to help make seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers are pretty parts that turn into fruits and seeds.

image.alt: Flowers - The Plant's Gift — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: A Bee Visits the Flowers
slides.storyContext: As Asha and Grandpa watch, a honeybee lands on a bright orange marigold. It buzzes and moves from flower to flower. 'What's the bee doing?' Asha wonders. Grandpa explains: 'The bee collects sweet nectar from flowers. But pollen sticks to its body. When it visits the next flower, pollen rubs off. That helps make seeds!' Asha watches in fascination.

points.text: Bees help flowers by moving pollen between them.
This process (pollination) leads to seeds and fruits.

slides.title: Fruits and Seeds - New Plants
slides.storyContext: Grandpa picks a ripe mango. Inside are seeds. 'A new mango tree can grow from this seed,' he says.

points.label: What are fruits?
points.text: Fruits grow from flowers and protect the seeds inside.

points.label: What are seeds?
points.text: Seeds can grow into new plants if they get soil, water, and sunlight.

points.label: From seed to plant
points.text: A tiny seed grows roots, a stem, leaves, then flowers—and the cycle repeats.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fruits protect seeds, and seeds grow into new plants.

image.alt: Fruits and Seeds - New Plants — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Planting a Mango Seed
slides.storyContext: Grandpa teaches Asha how to grow a new mango tree.

example.problem: Grandpa gives Asha a mango seed from the ripe fruit. To grow it into a plant, what does Asha need to do?
example.solution: Plant the seed in moist soil. Keep it warm. Water regularly. Place in sunlight after it sprouts. After 4-6 weeks, a small shoot will emerge. Asha will see a root growing down and a stem/leaves growing up!

points.text: Seeds need soil, water, warmth, and light to grow.
A seed contains a tiny plant inside just waiting to start.

slides.title: How a Tomato Plant Works
slides.storyContext: Asha watches Grandpa explain a whole tomato plant in the garden.

example.problem: Look at Grandpa's tomato plant. It has roots buried in the soil, a thick green stem, big leaves, yellow flowers, and red tomatoes. How does each part help the plant grow and make tomatoes?
example.solution: Roots drink water from soil. Stem carries water up to leaves and flowers. Leaves use sunlight to make food. Flowers turn into red tomatoes. The tomatoes protect seeds inside that can grow into new plants next year.

image.alt: How a Tomato Plant Works — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: The Plant Cycle Complete
slides.storyContext: Grandpa and Asha sit under the mango tree at sunset. 'This tree has roots underground drinking water. Its stem carries that water to leaves. Leaves catch sunlight and make food. That food helps make flowers. Flowers make seeds in fruits. And those seeds can grow into new trees!' Asha smiles. 'It's a never-ending circle!'

points.text: Plants have a complete life cycle from seed to plant to seed again.
Each part of the plant has a special job in this cycle.

slides.title: What Do You Know?
slides.storyContext: Grandpa gives Asha a riddle: 'I grow under the soil, drink water, and hold the plant tight. What am I?'

example.problem: Grandpa's riddle: 'I grow under the soil, drink water, and hold the plant tight. What am I?' And a second one: 'I am green, flat, and make food for the plant using sunlight. What am I?'
example.solution: First riddle: Roots. Second riddle: Leaves.

image.alt: What Do You Know? — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Design Your Own Garden
slides.storyContext: Asha is asked to plan a small vegetable garden.

example.problem: Plan a garden with tomatoes, spinach, and radishes. Consider: Where should roots have moist soil? When do flowers appear? When are fruits/seeds ready to harvest?
example.solution: All three need moist soil for roots. Tomato flowers appear in 6-8 weeks (red fruits in 12 weeks). Spinach leaves are harvestable in 4-6 weeks (no flowers needed). Radish roots swell in 4 weeks. Plant tomatoes deep. Water all regularly. Harvest at different times.

points.text: Different plants have different growth timelines.
Understanding plant parts helps us grow food.

slides.title: The Seasons Change
slides.storyContext: Months pass. Asha returns to Grandpa's garden in each season. She watches the mango tree: in spring it blooms with white flowers, in summer it bears green then yellow fruits, in autumn leaves turn yellow, and in winter it rests but roots stay alive underground, ready for spring.

points.text: Plants change with seasons but roots survive year-round.
The plant cycle repeats every year.

slides.title: Photosynthesis - How Plants Make Food
slides.storyContext: Grandpa explains the amazing process that happens inside leaves.

points.text: Photosynthesis is the process of making plant food.

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves are like tiny factories that turn sunlight into food using water and air.

slides.title: Why Plants Need Light
slides.storyContext: Asha asks why Grandpa keeps some plants in sunny spots and others in shade.

example.problem: Grandpa has a spinach plant in full sun and one in deep shade. After 4 weeks, which is bigger and greener?
example.solution: The one in full sun is bigger and greener. Why? More sunlight = more photosynthesis = more food made = faster growth and darker green leaves. The shaded plant grows slowly and has pale leaves.

points.text: More light = more photosynthesis = faster growth.
Even low-light plants need SOME light.

slides.title: Pollination Day
slides.storyContext: Asha spends the afternoon watching insects visit flowers. Bees buzz from flower to flower. A butterfly lands on a chili bloom. Grandpa whispers: 'Each visitor carries pollen. Without them, no seeds would form. No seeds means no new plants next year!'

points.text: Pollinators are essential for plant reproduction.
Without insects, many plants couldn't make seeds.

slides.title: Types of Roots
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Asha different plants with different root systems.

points.text: Root shape matches the plant's needs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different plants have different root shapes for different jobs.

slides.title: Challenge: Grow a Bean in a Jar
slides.storyContext: Grandpa gives Asha a challenge—grow a bean in a clear jar to see all the parts.

example.problem: Place a bean between wet paper towel and clear jar wall. Water daily. Predict: when will you see roots? When will you see leaves? Record what you see each day for 3 weeks.
example.solution: Day 1-2: Bean swells. Day 3-4: roots appear at bottom (white tip). Day 5-7: roots grow longer. Day 7-10: stem grows up. Day 10-14: first leaves unfold. By week 3: small plant with roots, stem, and leaves visible!

points.text: Roots always grow down (gravity), stems always grow up (light).
All plant parts are present in the seed—they just grow bigger.

slides.title: Plants Around Us
slides.storyContext: Asha realizes plants are everywhere: in parks, backyards, forests, fields, even as indoor houseplants. 'Every plant I see now makes sense,' she tells Grandpa. 'I look at any plant and ask: where are its roots? What does its stem do? How do its leaves look? What color are its flowers?' Understanding plant parts helps her appreciate nature's genius.

points.text: Plants are constantly growing and adapting around us.
Knowing plant parts helps you understand the whole world better.

slides.title: Asha Becomes a Gardener
slides.storyContext: By summer, Asha has helped Grandpa grow vegetables, fruit trees, and flowers. She understands each part's job. She knows when to water, when to weed, when to expect flowers. She realizes: 'I'm not just helping plants grow. I'm reading the story that every plant tells through its roots, stems, leaves, and flowers.'

points.text: Understanding plant parts makes you a better gardener.
Every plant tells a story of growth and survival.

slides.title: What Asha Learned
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Asha sits under the mango tree with Grandpa, remembering everything.

points.text: Roots drink water and hold the plant in soil.
Stems carry water and hold up leaves and flowers.
Leaves make food from sunlight.
Flowers turn into fruits with seeds.
Seeds grow into new plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every part of a plant has an important job to help it grow and make new plants.

image.alt: What Asha Learned — Plants - Parts and Functions

subject: Science
title: Ravi's Healthy Meal Adventure
hook: Discover which foods keep your body strong and healthy!

slides.title: Food and Health
slides.storyContext: Ravi learns why eating right keeps him healthy, strong, and happy.

image.alt: Food and Health — Food and Health

slides.title: Ravi's Energy Drops
slides.storyContext: One morning, Ravi feels tired during cricket practice. His friend plays well, but Ravi can barely run. At school, Doctor Priya checks him. 'Ravi, your body needs the RIGHT food. Let's learn what healthy eating looks like.'

image.alt: Ravi's Energy Drops — Food and Health

slides.title: A Chat with the Doctor
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya asks Ravi what he had for breakfast. 'Just a glass of juice and some biscuits,' Ravi says. 'No wonder you're tired!' Doctor Priya sits him down. 'Your body is like a machine that needs fuel AND building materials. Juice and biscuits don't have everything you need.'

points.text: Different foods do different jobs in your body.
Breakfast sets you up for the whole day.

slides.title: Food Groups - Building Blocks
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi a poster of different foods: rice, eggs, fruits, oil, milk.

points.label: We need different foods
points.text: Not one food has everything. We must eat from all groups.

points.label: Five main groups
points.text: Grains (rice, bread), protein (eggs, lentils), vegetables, fruits, dairy (milk, yogurt).

points.label: Each does a job
points.text: Grains give energy. Protein builds muscles. Vegetables and fruits protect your body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat foods from all groups to get energy, strong muscles, and good health.

image.alt: Food Groups - Building Blocks — Food and Health

slides.title: The Food Groups In Your Fridge
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya walks Ravi through what a balanced kitchen looks like.

example.problem: Ravi's fridge has: milk, eggs, rice, carrots, apples, butter, and bread. Which food groups does he have?
example.solution: Milk = dairy. Eggs = protein. Rice = grains. Carrots = vegetables. Apples = fruit. Butter = oils/fats. Bread = grains. He's missing fresh vegetables and could use more variety, but has basic groups covered.

points.text: Most kitchens have foods from most groups.
Balancing meals means choosing from each group.

slides.title: Energy Foods - Grains and Carbs
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mummy makes rotli from wheat flour. Doctor Priya explains why.

points.label: What are they?
points.text: Rice, wheat, bread, pasta—all grains that grow in fields.

points.label: What do they do?
points.text: They give your body energy to run, play, think, and study.

points.label: How much?
points.text: Eat grains at breakfast, lunch, and dinner—your body needs energy all day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Grains are the fuel that keeps you running and playing.

image.alt: Energy Foods - Grains and Carbs — Food and Health

slides.title: Energy for Cricket
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya explains: 'During cricket, your muscles burn energy. Where does that energy come from? From grains! When you eat rice or bread, your body breaks it down into glucose. Your muscles use glucose to move fast and hit the ball hard.'

points.text: Grains are converted into glucose in your body.
Glucose fuels every movement you make.

slides.title: Body-Building Foods - Protein
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya asks Ravi: 'Why are your muscles growing strong?' 'I eat eggs and drink milk!' he says proudly.

points.label: What is protein?
points.text: It's in eggs, milk, meat, lentils, beans—foods that build and repair muscles.

points.label: Why do we need it?
points.text: Protein helps your muscles grow big and strong. It repairs your body when you get hurt.

points.label: Where to find it
points.text: Eggs, milk, yogurt, paneer, chicken, fish, lentils, beans.

slides.inSimpleWords: Protein is like building blocks that make your muscles strong.

image.alt: Body-Building Foods - Protein — Food and Health

slides.title: Protein for Growing Bodies
slides.storyContext: Ravi is growing, and his body needs protein to build new muscle.

example.problem: Ravi plays cricket 3 times a week. His muscles get tiny micro-tears during play. What does his body need to repair them and grow stronger?
example.solution: Protein! When Ravi eats protein (eggs, milk, paneer, dal), his body uses it to repair muscle fibers. Over time, muscles grow back stronger. That's why athletes eat lots of protein.

points.text: Muscles need protein to repair and grow.
Daily protein = faster recovery from exercise.

slides.title: Protect & Defend - Fruits and Vegetables
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mummy packs him a lunch box with carrots, spinach, and an apple. 'These keep you healthy,' she says.

points.label: What do they have?
points.text: Vitamins and minerals that protect your body from getting sick.

points.label: Colors mean
points.text: Orange carrots have vitamin A for good eyes. Green spinach has iron for strong blood. Red apples have vitamin C.

points.label: Eat the rainbow
points.text: Different colors = different protections. Eat red, green, yellow, orange fruits and veggies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fruits and vegetables are like a shield protecting you from illness.

image.alt: Protect & Defend - Fruits and Vegetables — Food and Health

slides.title: Vitamins in the Lunch Box
slides.storyContext: Ravi opens his lunch box and sees colors. 'Orange carrots, green spinach, red tomato, yellow mango,' his mummy says. 'Each color has different vitamins. Together, they keep every part of your body working well—your eyes, bones, blood, immune system, everything!'

points.text: Each color provides different nutrients.
Colorful meals = complete nutrition.

slides.title: Healthy Habits - Water and Cleanliness
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi something surprising. 'This is as important as food!'

points.label: Drink water
points.text: Your body is mostly water. Drink clean water all day to stay healthy and strong.

points.label: Wash your hands
points.text: Before eating and after playing, wash hands with soap to remove germs.

points.label: Eat clean food
points.text: Wash fruits and vegetables. Cook meat and eggs fully. Store food in clean containers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clean water and clean hands keep bad germs away from your food.

image.alt: Healthy Habits - Water and Cleanliness — Food and Health

slides.title: The Power of Water
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya teaches Ravi why water is essential.

example.problem: Ravi plays cricket for 2 hours under the sun. He doesn't drink water during the game. By the end, he feels dizzy and tired. Why?
example.solution: He lost water through sweat. His body couldn't cool itself properly. His muscles didn't work well without water. Lesson: drink water before, during, and after exercise. Aim for 6-8 glasses daily, more on hot days and after sports.

points.text: Water helps your body stay cool through sweating.
Water carries nutrients to cells and removes waste.
Dehydration = fatigue, dizziness, poor performance.

slides.title: Ravi's Perfect Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: With help from Doctor Priya, Ravi plans a healthy day.

example.problem: Ravi wants to eat healthily all day. Plan his breakfast, lunch, snack, and dinner using all food groups.
example.solution: Breakfast: milk with oatmeal and sliced banana (grain, dairy, fruit). Snack: handful of almonds and an orange (protein, fruit). Lunch: rice with lentil dal, spinach curry, and cucumber salad (grain, protein, vegetable). Dinner: rotli with paneer and cooked carrots (grain, protein, vegetable). All day: drink water.

image.alt: Ravi's Perfect Day of Eating — Food and Health

slides.title: Ravi's First Week
slides.storyContext: For one week, Ravi eats balanced meals with all food groups. He drinks lots of water. He washes his hands before eating. By the end of the week, he has more energy during cricket practice. His friends notice: 'You're faster and stronger, Ravi!' He smiles. Good food works!

points.text: Balanced eating shows results in just one week.
Energy, strength, and focus all improve with good nutrition.

slides.title: Spot the Healthy Meal
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi three lunch boxes. Which one is healthiest?

example.problem: Box A: Only samosas and soda. Box B: Rice, dal, spinach, apple, and water. Box C: Only chocolate and chips. Which lunch box is the healthiest and why?
example.solution: Box B is healthiest. It has grains (rice), protein (dal), vegetables (spinach), fruit (apple), and water. It covers all food groups and has no junk food.

image.alt: Spot the Healthy Meal — Food and Health

slides.title: Design Your Ideal Weekly Menu
slides.storyContext: Ravi is challenged to plan his own healthy week.

example.problem: Plan a 3-day menu (breakfast, lunch, dinner) that includes all food groups, fits Indian meals your family makes, and keeps energy high for sports.
example.solution: Day 1: Breakfast—dosa with sambar (grain, vegetable). Lunch—rice, dal, okra (grain, protein, vegetable). Dinner—roti, paneer bhurji, cucumber (grain, protein, vegetable). Similar variety for Days 2-3 with different grains (wheat, bajra) and veggies. All meals include fruits/milk. All include water.

points.text: Planning meals ahead ensures balanced nutrition.
Variety keeps meals interesting and nutritious.

slides.title: Junk Food Trap
slides.storyContext: Ravi's friend Arjun loves samosas and sodas. Doctor Priya explains why too much junk food is dangerous: 'Junk food has lots of sugar, salt, and oil, but few vitamins or minerals. Your body becomes weak and gains extra weight. You get tired, your teeth decay, and your energy drops.'

points.text: Junk food fills you up but doesn't nourish you.
Too much junk food leads to health problems.

slides.title: Reading Food Labels
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya teaches Ravi to read packages and understand what he's eating.

points.text: Smart eating starts with reading what's on the package.

slides.inSimpleWords: Food labels tell you exactly what's inside so you can make smart choices.

slides.title: Comparing Two Cereals
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares two breakfast cereals at the store.

example.problem: Cereal A: 30g sugar per 100g, lots of additives, bright colors. Cereal B: 5g sugar per 100g, whole grains listed first, few additives. Which is healthier?
example.solution: Cereal B is much healthier. It has way less sugar (5g vs 30g) and whole grains provide energy without the crash. Cereal A is basically candy disguised as breakfast.

points.text: Lower sugar = better for energy and health.
Whole grains are real food, not processed.

slides.title: Ravi's Two-Month Journey
slides.storyContext: After 2 months of balanced eating, water, and exercise, Ravi returns to Doctor Priya. 'I can run faster! I scored better in math tests! My skin is clearer!' Doctor Priya smiles. 'That's nutrition and hydration working together. Your brain got better nutrients, your body got fuel and water. Everything improved!'

points.text: Good nutrition affects your whole body and mind.
Changes happen in weeks, not days—be patient and consistent.

slides.title: Digestion - From Mouth to Stomach
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya explains the journey food takes inside your body.

points.text: Digestion is a complex process that takes hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body breaks down food into tiny parts so it can absorb the good stuff.

slides.title: Why We Chew Our Food
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks why his mummy always says 'chew properly.'

example.problem: Ravi gulps his food in 2 minutes vs chewing it slowly for 20 minutes. Which is better and why?
example.solution: Slow chewing is much better. Chewing breaks food into tiny pieces (bigger surface area), saliva mixes in (starts digestion), and slow eating gives your brain time to signal 'full.' Result: better digestion, more nutrients absorbed, less likely to overeat.

points.text: Proper chewing = better digestion and nutrition.
Eating slowly = eating smarter.

slides.title: Food Choices Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices food choices in his daily life: school tiffin, restaurant menus, snack shops, birthday parties. 'Now I understand every food choice has consequences,' he thinks. 'I can pick samosa or salad. Chocolate or apple. Soda or water. Each choice affects my energy and health.' He feels empowered—he's not just eating, he's making smart decisions.

points.text: Every food choice matters, even small ones.
Knowledge gives you power to choose better.

slides.title: Ravi Teaches His Parents
slides.storyContext: Ravi comes home excited. He teaches his parents everything: the food groups, why vitamins matter, how to read labels. His mummy laughs. 'My son is now the food expert in this house!' Soon the whole family is eating balanced meals and drinking more water.

points.text: Healthy habits spread through families.
Knowledge shared is power shared.

slides.title: Ravi's Health Promise
slides.storyContext: Ravi feels stronger now. He tells Doctor Priya his plan to stay healthy.

points.text: Eat foods from all groups: grains, protein, vegetables, fruits, and dairy.
Eat different colored foods to get all vitamins and minerals.
Drink plenty of clean water every day.
Wash hands and keep food clean.
Eat healthy to run faster, think better, and stay strong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eating right makes you healthy, strong, smart, and happy.

image.alt: Ravi's Health Promise — Food and Health

subject: Science
title: Meera's Sky Adventure
hook: Explore the air we breathe, water we drink, and weather above us!

slides.title: Air, Water, Weather
slides.storyContext: Meera discovers the invisible air, precious water, and changing weather around her village.

image.alt: Air, Water, Weather — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: Meera's Flying Kite
slides.storyContext: Meera flies a kite on a windy day. She can't see the wind, but she feels it push her kite. 'What IS this wind?' she wonders. Teacher Singh smiles. 'That's air moving. Let me show you how air works and shapes our weather.'

slides.title: What is Air?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh fills a balloon with air. 'Air is all around us, but we can't see it. Yet it's real!'

points.label: Air is invisible
points.text: You can't see air, but it fills every space around us.

points.label: We breathe air
points.text: Inside air is oxygen—we breathe it in to live.

points.label: Air has weight
points.text: Air pushes in all directions. This push is called air pressure.

points.label: Air moves
points.text: Moving air is wind. It can push things like kites, boats, and leaves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air is an invisible gas all around us that we breathe and that makes wind.

slides.title: Feeling the Invisible
slides.storyContext: Meera closes her eyes and holds a plastic bag, then opens it. 'I see nothing but I FEEL something inside!' Teacher Singh nods. 'That's air filling the bag. Feel it push against the plastic.'

slides.title: Oxygen - The Air We Need
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh lights a candle inside a glass jar and covers it. 'Watch what happens when air runs out.'

points.label: What is oxygen?
points.text: Oxygen is a gas inside air that all animals need to breathe.

points.label: Plants make oxygen
points.text: Trees and plants produce oxygen from sunlight. Animals need this oxygen.

points.label: We breathe it in
points.text: When you breathe, your lungs take oxygen from air into your blood.

points.label: It keeps us alive
points.text: Without oxygen, a candle goes out. Without oxygen, animals can't survive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oxygen is the special part of air that we must breathe to stay alive.

slides.title: Air Pressure Experiment
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh fills a bottle with water, seals it with paper, and flips it upside down over a bucket. The paper stays on!

example.problem: Why does the paper stick to the bottle when Teacher Singh flips it upside down? The water should fall out!
example.solution: Air pressure from below pushes up on the paper harder than the water pushes down. The invisible air is strong enough to hold the water. Air has weight and pushes in all directions.

slides.title: Water - Life's Liquid
slides.storyContext: Meera and Teacher Singh walk to the well to get drinking water.

points.label: Where is water?
points.text: Water is in lakes, rivers, wells, oceans, and clouds.

points.label: We need water
points.text: All living things—people, plants, animals—need water to survive.

points.label: Water covers Earth
points.text: Oceans, rivers, and lakes cover most of Earth's surface.

points.label: Water changes form
points.text: Water can be liquid (rivers), solid (ice), or gas (steam and clouds).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is the precious liquid that all life on Earth needs.

slides.title: Three Forms of Water
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh boils water in a pot. 'Look—steam rising! That's water as a gas. And in winter, water freezes into ice. One thing, three shapes.'

slides.title: The Water Cycle
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh draws a diagram showing water rising, forming clouds, and falling as rain.

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes. Water rises as invisible vapor.

points.label: Condensation
points.text: High in the cold sky, vapor cools and becomes tiny water droplets. These form clouds.

points.label: Precipitation
points.text: When clouds get heavy, droplets fall as rain, snow, or sleet back to Earth.

points.label: Collection
points.text: Rain runs into rivers and oceans. The cycle begins again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water rises from oceans, forms clouds, falls as rain, and the journey repeats forever.

slides.title: Weather - Air on the Move
slides.storyContext: Dark clouds gather in the sky. Teacher Singh points up. 'Weather is what the air and sky are doing right now.'

points.label: What is weather?
points.text: Weather is the condition of air and sky at any moment—sunny, rainy, windy, hot, cold.

points.label: Weather changes
points.text: Air temperature, wind, clouds, and rain change throughout the day and seasons.

points.label: We observe weather
points.text: We see clouds, feel wind, measure temperature, and watch for rain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weather is what we see and feel in the sky and air each day.

slides.title: Monsoon Coming
slides.storyContext: Meera smells the air before the monsoon. 'It smells different. The wind changed. The clouds are dark.' Teacher Singh smiles. 'Yes, the weather is shifting. Your senses are alert.'

slides.title: Rain - Water Falling from Clouds
slides.storyContext: Rain begins to fall. 'Where does rain come from?' Meera asks. Teacher Singh explains the water cycle.

points.label: How does rain form?
points.text: Water from oceans and rivers rises as invisible vapor. It cools in the sky and forms clouds.

points.label: Clouds hold droplets
points.text: Tiny water droplets cluster together in clouds, getting heavier.

points.label: Rain falls
points.text: When droplets are too heavy, they fall as rain back to Earth.

points.label: Cycle repeats
points.text: Rain feeds rivers and oceans, then evaporates again—the water cycle goes on.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rain is water from oceans and rivers falling from clouds in the sky.

image.alt: Rain - Water Falling from Clouds — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: A Day of Weather
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh describes what happens on a typical monsoon day in the village.

example.problem: In the morning, it's hot and still. By noon, dark clouds arrive. By afternoon, strong wind blows and heavy rain falls. Water flows in streams. By evening, wind stops and sun appears. Explain what is happening to air, water, and weather.
example.solution: Morning: still, warm air and high temperature. Noon: water vapor rises from fields and rivers, cools high in sky, forms clouds. Afternoon: pressure difference causes wind to blow; condensed water falls as rain. Wind carries the rain over the land. Evening: storm passes, air cools, wind stops, water drains away, sun breaks through clouds.

image.alt: A Day of Weather — Air, Water, Weather

slides.title: Wind - Moving Air
slides.storyContext: The wind grows stronger. Meera's dupatta flutters. Teacher Singh says wind is air that moves.

points.label: What causes wind?
points.text: When air heats or cools unevenly, it moves from one place to another.

points.label: Wind has power
points.text: Strong wind can move leaves, dust, water, and even fly kites and sailing boats.

points.label: Different speeds
points.text: A breeze is gentle. A storm wind is fast and powerful.

points.label: We use wind
points.text: Windmills use wind to pump water. Sails use wind to move boats.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wind is air that moves because of heat differences. It can push and carry things.

slides.title: Hot and Cold Make Wind
slides.storyContext: Meera stands near a cooking fire and feels warm air rising. Then she steps into shade and feels cooler. Teacher Singh: 'That's how wind starts—hot air rises, cool air rushes in to replace it.'

slides.title: Temperature - Hot and Cold
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh brings a thermometer. 'This measures how hot or cold the air is. We call that temperature.'

points.label: Temperature measures heat
points.text: Thermometers show how hot or cold something is—in degrees.

points.label: Sun heats air
points.text: Sunlight warms the air. Hotter air is lighter and rises.

points.label: Night cools air
points.text: When the Sun sets, air loses heat and cools. Cool air sinks.

points.label: This creates wind
points.text: Moving between hot and cold areas creates wind and weather changes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature tells us how hot or cold the air is. Hot air rises, cold air sinks, and that makes wind.

slides.title: Guess the Weather
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh gives Meera clues to guess what weather is coming.

example.problem: Dark clouds are gathering. The wind is blowing hard. The air feels cool and damp. What weather is coming? And what should Meera do to stay safe?
example.solution: Rain and possibly a storm are coming. Meera should: bring the kite indoors, move away from trees, go inside the house, close windows and doors, stay inside until the storm passes.

slides.title: Reading the Sky
slides.storyContext: Meera learns to read clouds and predict weather. 'See those dark, fluffy clouds? Rain is coming. See those thin, wispy clouds? The weather will stay clear.'

slides.title: Types of Clouds
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh points to different clouds in the sky.

points.label: Cumulus clouds
points.text: Puffy white clouds that look like cotton. They mean fair weather.

points.label: Stratus clouds
points.text: Flat, gray layers that cover the whole sky. Light rain often falls from these.

points.label: Cirrus clouds
points.text: Thin, wispy clouds high in the sky. They don't bring rain soon.

points.label: Cumulonimbus clouds
points.text: Dark, towering storm clouds. Heavy rain, thunder, and lightning come from these.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different cloud shapes tell us different weather. Puffy clouds mean fair weather. Dark clouds mean rain or storms.

slides.title: Monsoon vs Summer
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh compares two seasons in the village.

example.problem: Describe the difference between a summer day and a monsoon day in Meera's village. Think about air, wind, clouds, rain, and temperature.
example.solution: Summer: hot, still air, bright sun, few clouds, no rain, high temperature, air feels dry. Monsoon: cooler air, strong wind, dark clouds, heavy rain, streams flowing, temperature drops, air feels damp. Wind brings moist air from the ocean. Rain falls because clouds are full of water vapor.

slides.title: Storm Safety
slides.storyContext: Meera and her friends take shelter during a thunderstorm. Teacher Singh teaches them what to do when dangerous weather arrives.

slides.title: Dangerous Weather
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh explains storms and how they form.

points.label: Thunderstorms
points.text: Strong, fast-moving clouds with heavy rain, strong wind, thunder, and lightning. Stay inside during storms.

points.label: Lightning is electricity
points.text: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity in the sky. Never stand outside or under trees during storms.

points.label: Hail can form
points.text: In very cold, tall clouds, water freezes into ice balls that fall. This is called hail.

points.label: Safety first
points.text: Listen to weather reports, prepare supplies, and follow safety rules during extreme weather.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some weather is dangerous. Storms bring heavy rain, lightning, and strong wind. Know how to stay safe.

slides.title: Dew and Frost
slides.storyContext: In the early morning, Meera notices water droplets on grass and spider webs. 'Is it rain?' she asks. Teacher Singh smiles. 'No, that's dew. It forms when water vapor condenses on cool surfaces at night.'

slides.title: Dew, Frost, and Fog
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh explains what happens when water vapor cools near Earth's surface.

points.label: Dew
points.text: Water vapor condenses into tiny droplets on grass, leaves, and webs at night and early morning.

points.label: Frost
points.text: When dew freezes into ice crystals on a very cold night, we see frost on the ground.

points.label: Fog
points.text: When condensation happens near the ground in the air, we see fog—tiny water droplets floating.

points.label: Part of the water cycle
points.text: Dew, frost, and fog are all water from the cycle, forming close to Earth's surface.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dew and frost form when water vapor cools near the ground. Fog is like a cloud at ground level.

slides.title: Water Cycle Complete
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh draws a complete circle showing the full journey of one water drop.

example.problem: Trace the journey of a water drop from the ocean to Meera's well and back. Name each step in the water cycle.
example.solution: Evaporation: Ocean water is heated by Sun, rises as vapor. Condensation: Vapor cools high in sky, becomes cloud. Precipitation: Cloud droplets fall as rain over land. Collection: Rain flows into rivers and wells, fills aquifers. Evaporation again: Sun heats water, cycle repeats. One drop may take days, months, or years for a complete cycle.

slides.title: Predict Weather from Clues
slides.storyContext: Teacher Singh shows Meera how to be a weather detective by observing multiple clues.

example.problem: Meera observes: the air is very humid (damp), wind is increasing, temperature dropped suddenly, and cumulonimbus clouds are forming in the west. What weather is coming in the next 2 hours? What should farmers do?
example.solution: A severe thunderstorm is coming soon. Farmers should: bring animals to shelter, secure loose items, check irrigation systems, stay alert for hail, avoid open fields during the storm. The damp air + wind + temperature drop + tall dark clouds = classic thunderstorm signals.

slides.title: What Meera Learned
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets and the rain stops, Meera watches a rainbow. She feels the light breeze.

points.text: Air is invisible but real. We breathe it, and it creates wind.
Water is found in oceans, rivers, lakes, wells, clouds, and rain.
Weather is what the air and sky do: sunny, rainy, windy, hot, or cold.
Rain comes from the water cycle: water rises, forms clouds, falls as rain.
Wind is air that moves because hot and cold air create movement.
Temperature, clouds, and air pressure help us predict and understand weather.
Dangerous weather like thunderstorms needs preparation and quick response.

slides.inSimpleWords: Air, water, and weather are always changing and shaping the world around us.

image.alt: What Meera Learned — Air, Water, Weather

subject: Science
title: Arun's Market Discovery
hook: Learn about materials we use every day—and what they're made of!

slides.title: Materials Around Us
slides.storyContext: Arun visits the market and discovers that everything is made of different materials.

image.alt: Materials Around Us — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Exploring the Market
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother takes him to the market. He sees clothes, pots, toys, and food everywhere. His sister picks up a wooden toy, then a metal spoon. 'Why is this one hard and this one softer?' she asks. Shopkeeper Uncle smiles. 'Because they are made of different materials! Let me show you.'

image.alt: Exploring the Market — Materials Around Us

slides.title: What is a Material?
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle gathers different objects—a clay pot, a steel knife, a cloth bag, and a wooden box.

points.label: Material means
points.text: The 'stuff' something is made from. Like clay, steel, cloth, wood, plastic.

points.label: Everything has a material
points.text: Your shirt is cloth. A pot is clay or metal. A toy is plastic or wood.

points.label: Materials have properties
points.text: Some are hard. Some are soft. Some are bendy. Some are shiny. Each material is different.

slides.inSimpleWords: A material is what something is made of. Different materials feel and look different.

image.alt: What is a Material? — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Touch and Feel
slides.storyContext: Arun closes his eyes and touches different materials. 'This is rough. This is smooth. This is cold. This is warm.' His sister laughs. 'You're learning with your hands!'

slides.title: Properties of Materials
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle creates a chart showing how different materials behave.

points.label: Hardness
points.text: Some materials are hard (wood, metal, glass). Some are soft (cloth, foam, rubber).

points.label: Flexibility
points.text: Some can bend without breaking (cloth, paper, rubber). Some snap if you bend them (glass, metal).

points.label: Texture
points.text: Surface can be smooth (glass), rough (cloth), or bumpy (wood).

points.label: Transparency
points.text: Some let light through (glass, clear plastic). Some block light (metal, wood).

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials have different properties: they can be hard or soft, smooth or rough, clear or opaque.

slides.title: Natural Materials - From Nature
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle shows Arun things that come directly from nature.

points.label: Wood from trees
points.text: Chairs, boxes, and sticks are made from wood. It's strong, can be carved, and burns.

points.label: Clay from earth
points.text: Pots, bricks, and dishes are made by digging clay from the ground and shaping it.

points.label: Wool from sheep
points.text: Sweaters and blankets are made from sheep's wool. It's warm and soft.

points.label: Cotton from plants
points.text: Clothes and bags are made from cotton. It grows in fields, is soft, and breathes well.

slides.inSimpleWords: Natural materials come directly from nature—like wood, clay, wool, and cotton.

slides.title: Where Wood Comes From
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle shows a wooden spoon and wooden chair. 'Both come from trees. Wood is strong, so we carve it into many shapes. And it's warm to hold.'

slides.title: From Plant to Cloth
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle traces how cotton becomes clothing.

example.problem: Arun's shirt is cotton. Explain the journey from cotton plant to wearing the shirt.
example.solution: Cotton grows in fields as fluffy white fiber. Workers pick the cotton. Machines separate seeds from fiber. The fiber is spun into thread. Thread is woven into cloth on looms. The cloth is sewn into a shirt. Arun's mother washes and wears it.

slides.title: Metals - Strong and Shiny
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle pulls out a steel spoon, a brass bell, and an aluminum pot.

points.label: What are metals?
points.text: Hard, shiny materials dug from under Earth. Iron, steel, copper, brass, aluminum.

points.label: Properties of metal
points.text: They are hard, shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and can be bent.

points.label: How we use metals
points.text: Spoons, pots, pans, bells, coins, jewelry, tools, cars.

slides.inSimpleWords: Metals are hard, shiny materials we dig from Earth and use for tools and dishes.

image.alt: Metals - Strong and Shiny — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Metals Get Hot Fast
slides.storyContext: Arun's sister puts a metal spoon in hot water. 'Ouch! It's hot!' Shopkeeper Uncle: 'Metal conducts heat—it moves heat from one place to another quickly.'

slides.title: Plastic - A Human-Made Material
slides.storyContext: Arun's sister grabs a plastic water bottle and a toy car. 'These don't come from nature,' Shopkeeper Uncle says.

points.label: What is plastic?
points.text: Plastic is made by humans from oil. It's light, strong, and doesn't break easily.

points.label: Why use plastic?
points.text: It's cheap, water-proof, and we can mold it into any shape—bottles, toys, bags, buckets.

points.label: A problem
points.text: Plastic doesn't rot away. It stays in Earth for hundreds of years. We should reuse it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plastic is made by humans and can be shaped into anything. But it takes forever to break down.

slides.title: Recycling Plastic
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle shows old plastic bottles being collected. 'These don't disappear. So we recycle them—melt and reshape into new bottles or other things.'

slides.title: Glass - Clear and Hard
slides.storyContext: A glass window in the shop catches sunlight. Shopkeeper Uncle taps it gently.

points.label: What is glass?
points.text: Glass is made by heating sand at very high temperatures.

points.label: Properties of glass
points.text: It's hard, clear, smooth, and you can see through it.

points.label: How we use it
points.text: Windows, drinking glasses, mirrors, jars, light bulbs.

points.label: Careful—
points.text: Glass is fragile and breaks easily into sharp pieces. Handle with care.

slides.inSimpleWords: Glass is made from sand and is clear, hard, and smooth—but breaks easily.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Material
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle asks Arun to pick materials for different jobs.

example.problem: What material would you use for: 1) a cooking pot (must conduct heat), 2) a water bottle (must be water-proof), 3) a window (must be clear), 4) a toy (must be safe and not break easily)?
example.solution: 1) Metal—conducts heat quickly to cook food. 2) Plastic—water-proof and light. 3) Glass—clear so you can see through it. 4) Wood or plastic—safe, won't shatter like glass.

slides.title: A Day in Materials
slides.storyContext: Arun's mother asks him to describe everything he used from morning to evening.

example.problem: From morning to evening, Arun uses many things: his cotton shirt, wooden school desk, steel spoon at breakfast, clay pot for water, plastic water bottle, glass window, metal door handle, and a wooden toy. Name the material each is made from and why it works well for that job.
example.solution: Cotton shirt: natural, soft, breathes well. Wooden desk: natural, strong, sturdy. Steel spoon: metal, hard, conducts heat, doesn't rust. Clay pot: natural, holds water, cool. Plastic bottle: human-made, light, water-proof. Glass window: clear, lets light in, hard. Metal handle: conducts heat, strong, durable. Wooden toy: natural, can be carved, warm to touch.

image.alt: A Day in Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Match the Material to the Job
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle plays a matching game with Arun.

example.problem: Match each job to the best material: 1) Making a raincoat. 2) Making a cooking pot. 3) Making a toy block. 4) Making a door handle. Options: Wood, metal, plastic, clay.
example.solution: 1) Raincoat = plastic (water-proof). 2) Cooking pot = metal (conducts heat well). 3) Toy block = wood (safe, warm to touch, can be carved). 4) Door handle = metal (strong and durable).

slides.title: Waste and Reuse
slides.storyContext: Arun notices Shopkeeper Uncle collecting scrap wood and metal. 'Nothing is truly waste. We can remake it into something new.'

slides.title: Biodegradable vs Non-biodegradable
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle explains what happens to materials over time.

points.label: Biodegradable
points.text: Natural materials like wood, cloth, paper, and food rot away in months or years.

points.label: Non-biodegradable
points.text: Plastic, glass, and metal don't rot away. They stay for centuries.

points.label: Impact on nature
points.text: We must be careful with non-biodegradable materials—they pile up as waste.

points.label: Solution: recycling
points.text: Melting and reshaping plastic, glass, and metal prevents waste and saves energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some materials rot naturally (wood, cloth). Others never break down (plastic, glass). We should recycle the ones that don't rot.

slides.title: A Shirt's Journey
slides.storyContext: Arun holds up his cotton shirt and thinks about all the steps from field to wearing it. His sister touches the soft fabric. 'Where does soft come from?'

slides.title: How Cloth is Made
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle explains textile manufacturing step by step.

points.label: From fiber to thread
points.text: Cotton fibers are combed, twisted together into long, strong threads.

points.label: Threads into fabric
points.text: Threads are woven or knitted together on looms to create flat sheets of cloth.

points.label: Dyeing and printing
points.text: Cloth is dipped in dyes to add color, or patterns are printed on with special inks.

points.label: Cutting and sewing
points.text: Cloth is cut into shapes and sewn together to make shirts, pants, dresses, and bags.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cotton fiber becomes thread, thread becomes cloth, and cloth becomes the clothes we wear.

slides.title: Testing Materials
slides.storyContext: Arun and his sister test materials with Shopkeeper Uncle. They tear paper, bend plastic, try to break glass, and dent metal. 'Each material behaves differently!'

slides.title: Comparing Properties
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle creates a chart comparing how materials behave under stress.

points.label: Tensile strength
points.text: How much pulling force before it breaks? Steel is very strong. String breaks easily.

points.label: Brittleness
points.text: Does it shatter suddenly? Glass is brittle. Wood can splinter. Plastic bends first.

points.label: Workability
points.text: Can we shape it easily? Clay is very workable. Metal must be heated. Glass is hard to shape.

points.label: Durability
points.text: How long does it last? Metal and glass last centuries. Paper rots in years. Plastic lasts 500+ years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials have different strengths and weaknesses. Some are strong, some are workable, and some last longer than others.

slides.title: Silk and Wool Stories
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle brings out a soft silk scarf and a warm wool blanket. 'These are even more special than cotton. They come from animals and are precious.'

slides.title: Animal-Derived Materials
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle explains silk, wool, leather, and fur.

points.label: Silk from silkworms
points.text: Silkworms spin cocoons from a protein thread. We unwind the cocoon to get long, smooth silk fiber.

points.label: Wool from sheep
points.text: Sheep grow thick, curly hair called fleece. We shear it, spin it into thread, weave into fabric.

points.label: Leather from animals
points.text: Animal hides are treated with chemicals, stretched, and dried to make strong leather.

points.label: Why they're valued
points.text: These materials are warm, durable, and have been used for thousands of years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Silk, wool, and leather are special natural materials that come from animals and are very durable.

slides.title: Design a Water Bottle
slides.storyContext: Shopkeeper Uncle asks Arun: 'If you were designing a new water bottle, what materials would you use for each part?'

example.problem: Design a water bottle choosing the best material for: 1) the main container (must hold water, be safe, last long), 2) the cap (must seal tightly, be easy to open), 3) the label (must show information, survive water). Which materials for each part?
example.solution: 1) Container = plastic or stainless steel (water-proof, lightweight, durable). 2) Cap = rubber or plastic (flexible to seal, easy to grip and turn). 3) Label = waterproof plastic or vinyl (doesn't fade when wet, sticks well). Together, they create a practical, safe product.

slides.title: Arun's Discovery
slides.storyContext: As they leave the market, Arun sees materials everywhere and understands what each is made of.

points.text: Materials are the stuff things are made from: wood, clay, metal, wool, cotton, plastic, glass.
Natural materials come from nature: wood, clay, wool, cotton, silk, leather.
Metal materials are hard, shiny, strong, and conduct heat.
Plastic is made by humans and is light, water-proof, and can be shaped.
Glass is made from sand and is clear, hard, but breaks easily.
Some materials rot away (biodegradable). Others stay forever (non-biodegradable). Recycling helps both.
Choosing the right material for a job depends on its properties—strength, flexibility, durability, and cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Everything around us is made of a material. Different materials have different properties and uses.

image.alt: Arun's Discovery — Materials Around Us

subject: Science
title: Kabir's Sky School
hook: Learn about Earth, the Sun, day and night, and seasons!

slides.title: The Earth and Sun
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ajay learn why we have day and night, and why seasons change throughout the year.

slides.title: Why Does the Sun Disappear?
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ajay sit on the rooftop watching the sunset. 'Where does the sun go at night?' Ajay asks. 'Will it come back tomorrow?' Teacher Lata joins them with a flashlight and globe. 'Let me show you how Earth and Sun move together.'

image.alt: Why Does the Sun Disappear? — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: What is the Sun?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shines the flashlight bright. 'This is like the Sun. A huge, hot star in the sky.'

points.label: The Sun is huge
points.text: It's a giant ball of hot, glowing gas that floats in space.

points.label: It gives light and heat
points.text: Light from the Sun reaches Earth, giving us day, warmth, and energy.

points.label: It's far away
points.text: The Sun is so far that light takes 8 minutes to reach us.

points.label: It never moves
points.text: The Sun stays in place. Earth moves around the Sun.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sun is a giant, hot, glowing star that gives Earth light and heat.

slides.title: The Sun Stays Still
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata holds the flashlight steady. 'The Sun doesn't move. We do. We're spinning around it like dancers around a lamp.'

slides.title: What is Earth?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata spins the globe slowly. 'This is Earth—and we live on it!'

points.label: Earth is round
points.text: Earth is a sphere—like a giant ball floating in space.

points.label: It rotates
points.text: Earth spins like a top, turning once every 24 hours.

points.label: It orbits the Sun
points.text: Earth moves around the Sun in a circle, taking 365 days (one year).

points.label: We're on the surface
points.text: We live on Earth's outer surface. Gravity holds us down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is a round planet that spins once a day and circles the Sun once a year.

image.alt: What is Earth? — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: We're Always Moving
slides.storyContext: Ajay is shocked. 'We're moving? But I'm sitting still!' Teacher Lata smiles. 'You ARE sitting still—but Earth is moving, and you're on it. You're moving with Earth at 30,000 kilometers per hour!'

slides.title: Day and Night - Earth Spinning
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata dims the lights and spins the globe while shining the flashlight on one side.

points.label: Why day and night?
points.text: As Earth spins, different parts face the Sun at different times.

points.label: Day side
points.text: The part facing the Sun gets light and warmth. That's daytime there.

points.label: Night side
points.text: The opposite side faces away and is in darkness. That's nighttime.

points.label: Rotation takes time
points.text: Earth takes 24 hours (one day) to spin once. That's why we have day and night.

slides.inSimpleWords: Day and night happen because Earth spins. Your side faces the Sun = day. Your side faces away = night.

slides.title: A Day on Earth
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata traces what happens to India in 24 hours as Earth spins.

example.problem: Describe what happens to Kabir's village over 24 hours of Earth's rotation.
example.solution: Morning 6 AM: India faces toward Sun, sunrise happens, day begins. Noon: Sun is highest in sky, shadows are shortest, daytime is brightest. Evening 6 PM: India turns away from Sun, sunset happens. Midnight: India faces completely away, dark night. Morning again: India rotates back to face Sun, sunrise happens again.

slides.title: Seasons - Earth's Tilted Path
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shows how Earth tilts as it goes around the Sun. 'This tilt creates seasons!'

points.label: Earth is tilted
points.text: Earth doesn't stand straight. It tilts at an angle of 23.5 degrees.

points.label: Summer and Winter
points.text: When your part tilts toward the Sun = summer (hot, long days). When it tilts away = winter (cold, short days).

points.label: Spring and Fall
points.text: As Earth orbits, the tilt changes: spring and fall are in-between seasons.

points.label: Cycle repeats
points.text: After 365 days, Earth completes one orbit and the cycle repeats. Seasons happen again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Seasons change because Earth is tilted and orbits the Sun. Tilt toward Sun = summer. Tilt away = winter.

slides.title: Summer Heat
slides.storyContext: In summer, Kabir feels the intense heat. Teacher Lata explains: 'India is tilted toward the Sun. The Sun's rays hit straight down. That's why it's so hot.'

slides.title: Why Does Tilt Matter?
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata uses an angle board to show how sunlight hits Earth differently in summer vs winter.

points.label: Direct rays = hot
points.text: When the Sun's rays come straight down (summer), they give more heat to a smaller area.

points.label: Slanted rays = less hot
points.text: When the Sun's rays come at an angle (winter), they spread out. Less heat reaches the ground.

points.label: Day length changes
points.text: Summer has long days because your part of Earth faces the Sun for more hours.

points.label: Combined effect
points.text: Direct rays PLUS long days = very hot summer. Slanted rays PLUS short days = very cold winter.

slides.inSimpleWords: In summer, the Sun's rays come straight down and days are long, so it's hot. In winter, rays come at an angle and days are short, so it's cold.

slides.title: Shadows and Sunlight
slides.storyContext: Kabir notices his shadow is long in the morning and short at noon. Teacher Lata explains.

points.label: Shadows change with time
points.text: As the Sun moves across the sky, shadows change direction and length.

points.label: Morning shadows
points.text: Sun is low on horizon = long shadow pointing away from Sun.

points.label: Noon shadows
points.text: Sun is high overhead = shadow is short and below the object.

points.label: Evening shadows
points.text: Sun is low again = long shadow pointing the opposite way.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shadows move and change size as the Sun moves across the sky during the day.

image.alt: Shadows and Sunlight — The Earth and Sun

slides.title: A Full Year's Journey
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata describes what happens to Earth over one complete year.

example.problem: Explain what happens to Kabir's village over one year: the length of days, temperature, and shadows as Earth orbits the Sun. Describe spring, summer, fall, and winter.
example.solution: Spring: Days get longer, temperature rises, shadows shorten at noon. Summer: Days are longest, very hot, noon shadows shortest. Fall: Days get shorter, temperature drops, shadows lengthen. Winter: Days are shortest, very cold, noon shadows longest. Then the cycle repeats. This happens because Earth's tilt makes different seasons as it orbits the Sun.

slides.title: Same Sun, Different Seasons
slides.storyContext: Ajay is confused. 'But the Sun is always the same distance away. So why does temperature change?' Teacher Lata nods. 'Good question! It's not the distance. It's the ANGLE of the rays and the LENGTH of the day.'

slides.title: The Four Seasons in Order
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata marks out Earth's path around the Sun, labeling each season.

points.label: Spring (March-May)
points.text: Northern Hemisphere tilts gradually toward Sun. Days get longer, temperature rises, flowers bloom.

points.label: Summer (June-August)
points.text: Northern Hemisphere tilts most toward Sun. Days are longest, very hot, intense sunlight.

points.label: Fall (September-November)
points.text: Northern Hemisphere tilts gradually away. Days get shorter, temperature drops, leaves fall.

points.label: Winter (December-February)
points.text: Northern Hemisphere tilts most away. Days are shortest, cold, sometimes snow falls.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spring and Fall are when the tilt is in-between. Summer is hottest. Winter is coldest.

slides.title: Predict the Time
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata points to different shadows and asks Kabir to guess the time of day.

example.problem: Look at shadows. Shadow 1 is very long pointing west. Shadow 2 is very short under the object. Shadow 3 is long pointing east. When in the day do these shadows happen?
example.solution: Shadow 1 (long, pointing west) = morning (Sun in the east). Shadow 2 (short) = noon (Sun high overhead). Shadow 3 (long, pointing east) = evening (Sun in the west).

slides.title: Different Places, Different Times
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shows that while it's noon in India, it's sunrise in Europe and midnight in America. 'Earth's rotation means every place has a different time at the same moment!'

slides.title: Equator vs Poles
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata compares weather at the equator and the North/South poles.

example.problem: Why is it hot all year at the equator, but cold all year at the North Pole? Both are on Earth, rotating together.
example.solution: At the equator, the Sun's rays come nearly straight down all year long, even when Earth is tilted. Tilt changes little. At the North Pole, the Sun's rays come at a steep angle all year. Even in summer, when the pole tilts toward the Sun, rays are still slanted. The tilt matters more where you are farther from the equator.

slides.title: Time Zones Around Earth
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shows a map and asks: 'Right now, it's noon here. In London, it's morning. In Tokyo, it's already night. Why?'

slides.title: Time Zones
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata explains how Earth's rotation creates different times across the planet.

points.label: Earth divides into zones
points.text: The world is divided into 24 time zones, one for each hour of Earth's rotation.

points.label: West to east
points.text: Moving east, time gets later. Moving west, time gets earlier. This is because Earth rotates west to east.

points.label: 24-hour cycle
points.text: As Earth spins 360 degrees in 24 hours, each zone is offset by 1 hour from its neighbor.

points.label: Date line
points.text: At the International Date Line (180 degrees), the date changes. It's the newest day east of the line, and the oldest day west of it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's rotation divides the world into 24 time zones. When it's noon in India, it's morning in Europe and night in America.

slides.title: Moon and Tides
slides.storyContext: Kabir asks: 'Why does the ocean level change twice a day?' Teacher Lata smiles. 'The Moon is pulling on Earth's water!'

slides.title: The Moon and Tides
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata explains the Moon's effect on Earth's oceans.

points.label: The Moon orbits Earth
points.text: Like Earth orbits the Sun, the Moon orbits Earth, taking about 29.5 days.

points.label: Gravity pulls water
points.text: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, making them bulge outward on the Moon-facing side.

points.label: Tides rise and fall
points.text: As Earth rotates, different places face the Moon, causing high tides (water rises) and low tides (water falls).

points.label: Twice per day
points.text: Most places have two high tides and two low tides every 24 hours as Earth spins.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's ocean water, making it rise and fall as tides, twice per day.

slides.title: Seasons Reversed
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata asks: 'What season is it in Australia right now?'

example.problem: When it's summer in India (June-August), what season is it in Australia, which is in the Southern Hemisphere?
example.solution: It's winter in Australia! When India tilts toward the Sun, Australia tilts away from the Sun. The Southern Hemisphere has opposite seasons from the Northern Hemisphere. When India has spring, Australia has fall. When India has summer, Australia has winter.

slides.title: Plan a Solar Observation
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata asks Kabir to plan how to track the Sun's position over one year.

example.problem: Design a year-long experiment to track how the Sun's position changes. Choose a location. Where will the Sun be highest in the sky? When will shadows be longest? How can you measure without hurting your eyes?
example.solution: Set up a gnomon (vertical stick) in a fixed location. Measure shadow length and direction daily at noon. Record data. In summer (June), shadow will be shortest and Sun highest. In winter (December), shadow will be longest and Sun lowest. Use a smartphone shadow app or photograph shadows carefully. Never look directly at the Sun.

slides.title: Day and Night Around Earth
slides.storyContext: Teacher Lata shows how at any moment, half of Earth is in daylight and half is in darkness.

points.label: Half lit, half dark
points.text: The Sun lights only one side of Earth at a time. The other side is in darkness.

points.label: Constant rotation
points.text: As Earth rotates, places move from night into day, then from day into night.

points.label: Terminator line
points.text: The line between day and night is called the terminator. It moves around Earth once every 24 hours.

points.label: Sunrise and sunset
points.text: When your location crosses the terminator moving toward the Sun = sunrise. Moving away = sunset.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth always has half day and half night. The line between them moves around Earth as it spins.

slides.title: Kabir's Cosmic Understanding
slides.storyContext: As stars appear in the night sky, Kabir feels connected to the cosmos.

points.text: The Sun is a giant hot star giving Earth light and heat.
Earth is a round planet that spins once per day (rotation).
Earth's rotation causes day and night as different parts face the Sun.
Earth orbits the Sun once per year. The tilt causes seasons.
Earth's tilt at 23.5 degrees creates the difference between summer and winter.
Shadows tell us the Sun's position and help us tell time.
Time zones exist because Earth rotates. It's different times in different places simultaneously.
The Moon orbits Earth and causes tides by pulling on ocean water.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth spins to make day and night. Earth orbits to make seasons. The Sun powers it all.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arun and Priya's Market Day Mystery
hook: Arun needs to count 40 mangoes fast. Priya shows him a shortcut.

slides.title: The Mango Basket Problem
slides.storyContext: Arun's father owns a fruit shop. Today he received 4 baskets of mangoes, with 8 mangoes in each basket. Arun tries counting on his fingers but gets confused. Priya arrives to help.

points.label: Scene
points.text: Sunday morning at Delhi fruit market. Baskets stacked near the shop counter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Arun counts 4 baskets with 8 mangoes each.

image.alt: The Mango Basket Problem — Multiplication

slides.title: Groups and Repeated Addition
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Instead of counting 8 + 8 + 8 + 8, we can say 4 groups of 8. That's 4 times 8.'

points.label: Idea
points.text: Multiplication means: equal groups of things

points.label: Symbol
points.text: 4 × 8 means 4 groups of 8

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication is quick repeated addition of groups.

image.alt: Groups and Repeated Addition — Multiplication

slides.title: Arun's Mango Count
slides.storyContext: Priya draws 4 circles, puts 8 dots in each. 'See? Add them all: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32. Or say 4 × 8 = 32.'

example.problem: 4 baskets, 8 mangoes each. How many total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Four times eight equals thirty-two mangoes total.

image.alt: Arun's Mango Count — Multiplication

slides.title: Times Tables Start Here
slides.storyContext: Arun learns: 4 × 1 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 4 × 3 = 12... Priya says, 'It's like counting by 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20...'

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Multiplying by 4: skip count 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32...

slides.inSimpleWords: Times tables are skip counting in equal groups.

image.alt: Times Tables Start Here — Multiplication

slides.title: Priya's Flower Pots
slides.storyContext: Priya mentions her garden: 'I have 6 pots with 3 flowers each. How many flowers do I have?'

example.problem: 6 pots with 3 flowers per pot. Total flowers?
example.solution: 6 × 3 = 18 flowers

slides.inSimpleWords: Six times three is eighteen flowers in total.

image.alt: Priya's Flower Pots — Multiplication

slides.title: Market Challenge
slides.storyContext: Arun's father asks: 'Arun, if I sell 5 bundles of 7 apples each, how many apples do I sell?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use groups: five groups of seven equals thirty-five.

image.alt: Market Challenge — Multiplication

slides.title: Order Doesn't Matter
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: '4 × 8 is the same as 8 × 4. Both give 32. You can flip the groups around.'

example.problem: Does 3 × 5 equal 5 × 3?
example.solution: Yes! Both = 15. Order of multiplication doesn't change the answer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the numbers; multiplication answer stays same.

image.alt: Order Doesn't Matter — Multiplication

slides.title: More Baskets Arrive
slides.storyContext: Suddenly, Arun's father gets a delivery: 3 more baskets, each with 10 mangoes! Arun says, 'That's 3 × 10. Can I use the same trick?'

points.label: New problem
points.text: Additional delivery: 3 baskets × 10 mangoes = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: Three baskets of ten mangoes—use multiplication again.

slides.title: Multiplying by 10 is Easy

slides.title: Birthday Party Fair Share
slides.storyContext: Priya's birthday party has 24 chocolates. She wants to give each friend the same number. There are 6 friends (including her). How many chocolates does each friend get? Arun says, 'That's division!'

slides.title: Division and Multiplication are Opposites
slides.storyContext: Arun says: 'If 6 × 4 = 24, then 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Multiplication groups; division ungroups.'

points.text: 24 things in 6 groups → divide: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 each

slides.storyContext: Priya: '1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 of one pizza.' Arun: 'And 5/8 - 2/8 = 3/8 of another!' They solve quickly using the rule.
slides.inSimpleWords: Practice adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions.

image.alt: Pizza Arithmetic — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Priya points out: 'Fractions are everywhere! Half a glass of milk, quarter hour on the clock, third of a cake, two-thirds full tank of petrol.'

points.label: Real use
points.text: Time (1/4 hour), volume (1/2 cup), temperature, cooking recipes

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole in daily life.

image.alt: Fractions in Real Life — Fractions

slides.title: Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arun gets confused: 'What if I eat 5/4 of a pizza? That's more than one whole!' Priya explains: '5/4 is called an improper fraction. It means 1 and 1/4 pizzas, or 1 1/4.'

points.label: Improper fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ denominator (5/4, 3/2, 7/5)

points.label: Mixed number
points.text: Whole number + fraction (1 1/4, 2 3/5)

points.label: Conversion
points.text: 5/4 = 1 1/4 (divide 5 by 4: quotient 1, remainder 1)

slides.inSimpleWords: Improper fractions have numerators bigger than or equal to denominators.

image.alt: Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers — Fractions

slides.title: Converting Mixed Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arun converts: '1 1/2 pizzas = ? Multiply 1 × 2 = 2, add the 1: (2+1)/2 = 3/2. So 1 1/2 = 3/2!'

example.problem: Convert 2 3/4 to an improper fraction

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions by multiplying.

image.alt: Converting Mixed Numbers — Fractions

slides.title: Final Pizza Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya's father brings a surprise: '2 pizzas cut into quarters. You have already eaten 5 quarters. How much pizza is left as a fraction?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 2 pizzas = 8 quarters. 8/4 - 5/4 = ? or 3/4 left?

slides.inSimpleWords: Two pizzas have eight quarters total; find the leftover amount.

image.alt: Final Pizza Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'Is 1/2 bigger than 2/5?' Arun draws both and realizes he needs a common denominator to compare fairly.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Comparing 1/2 and 2/5 requires different approach

points.label: Solution
points.text: Convert to common denominator: 1/2 = 5/10 and 2/5 = 4/10

slides.inSimpleWords: Use common denominators to compare different fractions.

image.alt: Comparing Fractions with Different Denominators — Fractions

slides.title: Converting to Compare
slides.storyContext: Priya practices: Compare 1/3 and 1/4. Common denominator is 12. 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12. So 1/3 > 1/4.

example.problem: Compare 2/3 and 3/5 using common denominator
example.solution: Common denominator is 15. 2/3 = 10/15, 3/5 = 9/15. So 2/3 > 3/5

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert both fractions to same denominator, then compare numerators.

image.alt: Converting to Compare — Fractions

slides.title: Master-Level Fraction Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's big challenge: 'I ate 1/3 of a pizza Monday, 1/4 of a pizza Tuesday. How much pizza did I eat in total?'

points.label: Try this
points.text: 1/3 + 1/4: common denominator is 12. 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12. Total = 7/12 pizza

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions with different denominators by finding common denominator.

image.alt: Master-Level Fraction Problem — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions Build Confidence
slides.storyContext: By week's end, Arun and Priya spot fractions everywhere with confidence. Music (3/4 time), recipes (1/2 cup), sports (first quarter), clocks (quarter past)—fractions unlock understanding!

points.label: Mastery
points.text: Fractions are the foundation for deeper math like algebra and percentages

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions connect to music, time, cooking, and advanced math.

image.alt: Fractions Build Confidence — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Arun and Priya see fractions all around: half a glass of milk, a quarter hour on the clock, three-quarters of a tank full.

points.label: Remember
points.text: Fraction = one or more equal parts of a whole

points.label: Remember
points.text: 1/2 (half), 1/3 (third), 1/4 (quarter) are common

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bottom number = how many equal pieces total

points.label: Remember
points.text: Bigger denominator = smaller each piece

points.label: Remember
points.text: Same denominator? Add numerators, keep denominator same

points.label: Remember
points.text: Equivalent fractions look different but mean the same

points.label: Remember
points.text: Improper fractions (5/4) can be written as mixed numbers (1 1/4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole in daily life.
